## How This Document Is Structured

Epics are grouped into three layers: **Foundation** (the core engine that all modes share), **Platform** (the extensibility, UI, and infrastructure layer that applications build on), and **Application** (the user-facing modes and interfaces). Cross-cutting concerns span all layers.

Story sizing uses T-shirt sizes: **S** (< 1 day), **M** (1-3 days), **L** (3-5 days), **XL** (1-2 weeks).

Stories sourced from the platform requirements document are tagged with their R-number origin (e.g. `[R2.3]`) for traceability.

### The story table schema

Every story table has exactly four columns — `| Story | Size | Status | Summary |` — and every story
row has exactly four cells and a closing `|`. A literal `|` inside a cell is written `\|`. This is not
housekeeping: `scripts/check_backlog.py` parses these rows, the SUMMARY below is generated from them,
and `docs/claims.md` is derived from that. Before RV1.7a eight epics used a three-column table with no
status column at all, carrying status as a trailing `**[Done]**` inside the Summary cell, which is why
two careful parses of this file once disagreed on its own row count.

**Status vocabulary — closed.** The Status cell is exactly one of the following, and nothing else. The
cell is capped at 120 characters; rationale longer than that belongs in the Summary, after
`**Status detail:**`.

| Status | Means |
|--------|-------|
| *(blank)* | Not started |
| `**Done**` | Done. Optionally followed by ` — <short note>`, usually a date |
| `**Reopened**` | Was marked Done, exercised, and found false. Optionally ` — <short reason>` |
| `**Partial**` | Some of it is done and the rest is named. Optionally ` — <short reason>` |
| `⏸ On hold — <reason>` | Blocked on something that is not a story: a missing toke capability, hardware. *(reserved — no row currently carries it)* |
| `Blocked — <ID or reason>` | Blocked on a named story, or on a stated non-story reason |
| `Queued behind <ID>` | Ordered after another story rather than blocked by it |
| `Superseded by <ID>` | The work moved wholesale into another story |

**What a `**Done**` marker must carry (RV1.7).** A row whose subject is runtime behaviour is Done
only when its Summary names the evidence that exercised it: the test file that asserts it against the
real module, or the command that was run and what it printed. "Implemented" is not evidence, and a
test that only reads the source is not a test of the behaviour. Where the assertion was proven able to
fail, say so, because a test nobody has seen fail is the thing this backlog was full of. A hygiene row
(a sweep, a rename) names the detector that now reports zero. This is a rule for reviewers, not a check.
No script can tell whether a named test really asserts what the row claims, which is why RV1 exists.

`Spec done` was in this legend until RV1.7a and appeared on **zero** rows, so it has been removed
rather than kept as an unused value. Reinstating it means adding it here and to the `STATUSES` table in
`scripts/check_backlog.py` in the same commit — the checker fails on a status that is not in both.

> **⏸ On hold** stories are blocked pending a dependency becoming ready for development. See the hold notice on each affected layer for detail. **The toolchain hold was cleared on 2026-09-20** and the build has been green since 2026-09-22 — so the only remaining holds are hardware (LC1), a genuinely missing toke capability, or another story. **Re-surveyed twice on 2026-09-23, and the second survey closes the category: `std.zip`, `std.toon` and `std.encrypt` are present at the pinned commit, and `std.xlsx`, `std.pdf` and `std.ocr` all landed just after it. So NO story in this document is now held on a missing toke capability** — the four asks in `docs/toke-libraries-required.md` (PDF, zip, XLSX, OCR) are all satisfied, and `std.ocr` binds macOS Vision directly so the standalone OCR repository it proposed is unnecessary. What remains is a `TOOLCHAIN.lock` decision, not a gap. The only real holds left are hardware (LC1) and other stories. As of that survey **no story row carries `⏸`** — X8.5, the last one, was released when NC1.9 landed.

# FOUNDATION LAYER

> **Foundation layer — now in development**
>
> loke is built on **ooke** ([github.com/karwalski/ooke](https://github.com/karwalski/ooke)) — a lightweight CMS and web application framework written in the toke programming language. **The toolchain hold was cleared on 2026-09-20** and [`TOOLCHAIN.lock`](../TOOLCHAIN.lock) is the authority. **The build is green as of 2026-09-22: 218 of 218 modules compile, 0 errors, and `packages/browser/build/loke` links.** The suite runs 122 of 122 passing. Superseded figures, recorded so they are not reinstated: "58 of 199 modules, 291 errors" (2026-09-20) and "217 of 217" (2026-09-22). **What green does not mean:** the build covers four roots and **247 non-test `.tk` files in six trees have never been compiled** (F10.23), and only 26 of 122 test files import a production module (X7). Remaining F10 work: F10.8, F10.12, F10.13, F10.15a, F10.16, F10.17, F10.20, F10.21, F10.22, F10.23.
>
> **Architectural impact of ooke:**
>
> | Previously specified | Replaced by |
> |---|---|
> | TypeScript (strict, ESM) | toke programming language |
> | pnpm workspaces monorepo | ooke build system (`ooke.toml`) |
> | Electron (browser mode app shell) | ooke native binary + web view |
> | Node.js runtime | ooke compiled native binary (C) |
> | ESLint / Prettier | toke linting and formatting tools |
> | Vitest test runner | toke test runner |
> | @electron/llm (in-process inference) | Native inference via ooke bindings |
> | Transformers.js (browser-side NER) | Local SLM via ooke native bindings |
> | compromise.js (JS NLP library) | NER via local SLM (language-agnostic) |
> | LanceDB (Node.js vector store) | Vector store via ooke native bindings |
> | better-sqlite3 / SQLCipher | SQLite + SQLCipher via ooke native bindings |
>
> What does **not** change: Ollama (REST API, language-agnostic), Presidio (Python sidecar via REST), MCP protocol (implemented in toke), the pipeline architecture, all functional requirements, and all acceptance criteria.

| F2.6 | XL | **Done** | Tiered inference engine (three tiers: Interactive — fully in GPU/unified memory, 25–55 tok/s, models up to 10B; Considered — partial GPU offload via Ollama `num_gpu`/llama.cpp `--n-gpu-layers`, 5–15 tok/s, up to 70B quantised; Background — maximum offload with heavy RAM/disk streaming, 0.5–5 tok/s, 70B+ full precision; tier selected by F5 router based on request source, user flag, task classification, and AG1 latency tolerance; progress indicator for Considered and Background; tier benchmarked on first run per model) |
| F2.7 | L | **Done** | Background inference queue (sequential job queue for Background-tier requests; priority: user-initiated > agent-scheduled > evaluation; Interactive always preempts — Background job pauses and resumes; `loke queue list/cancel/prioritise/pause/resume`; persists across restarts; completion notifications; queue metrics fed into G4 dashboards) |
| F2.8 | L | **Done** | Hardware-aware model recommendations (profile RAM, GPU VRAM, unified memory, disk type/speed, CPU on first run; per-model viability assessment at each inference tier; recommendations shown in model selector with tier badges; refreshed on hardware change, new model added, or companion device paired; `loke models recommend` CLI; disk space warnings) |
| F2.8a | M | **Done** — 2026-09-26 | **Hardware detection is a stub** — Found 2026-09-24 closing T7.3. `core.models.hardware.detect()` logs "stub -- returning Mac defaults" and returns a literal profile (16 GB unified, NVMe 3000 MB/s, 8 cores, macos) on every machine, and `detectprofile()`, which `packages/browser/pages/installer.tk` calls, returns `0`. So every recommendation F2.8 describes is computed from constants. F2.8 is marked Done; its hardware-profile clause is not. Needs a real probe (sysctl `hw.memsize`/`hw.ncpu` on macOS) behind a function that returns plain fields, not an f64 across a module boundary (T-20). **Done 2026-09-26.** `detect()` measures, through `std.sys`: RAM (`totalramgb`, whole GB), core count (`cpucount`), architecture and platform. On Apple silicon the memory is reported as unified. GPU VRAM, disk type and disk speed are NOT measured, and stay 0 or `$unknown`, meaning unknown and never invented. `detectprofile()` returns `detect()` instead of the integer 0. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/models/test_hardware.tk` compares against an INDEPENDENT measurement, `sysctl -n hw.ncpu` and `hw.memsize` spawned by the test itself, so it is not circular. With the old stub, the core-count and RAM assertions both FAILED and `detectprofile()` then aborted the process with RT005. The serialiser assertions now use a fixed profile: they had pinned the stub's literals (nvme, 8 cores). |
| F2.9 | L | **Done** | Disk-streaming inference for extreme offload (Background tier only; load model layers from NVMe sequentially with overlapped I/O prefetch; decompose large model into per-layer shards in `~/.loke/models/shards/`; configurable RAM ceiling; requires NVMe — warns on SATA/HDD; graceful degradation if < 0.1 tok/s; actual tok/s displayed with cloud cost comparison; equivalent of AirLLM layer-by-layer execution via llama.cpp mmap/partial-offload) |
| F2.10 | S | **Done** — 2026-09-24 | **With Ollama stopped, the Ollama client reported it running, and listing models killed the process** — Found 2026-09-24, once `/installer` returned its value (LS1.1u). (1) `core.models.ollama.healthcheck` used `http.get`, which returns `$ok` carrying a nil response against a closed port (T-15), so it answered 1, "running", whenever Ollama was down. It was also declared `:i64` while all five callers bound the result as `$ollamastatus`. It now checks `shared.reachability` first and returns the sum type. (2) `listmodels` and `listrunning` parsed that nil body and crashed. They now return an empty list when the service is unreachable; empty rather than `$err`, because T-18 would read a returned `$err` as `$ok` in every caller. (3) The installer page read RAM from `hw.detectprofile()`, a stub declared `:i64` that returns 0, so the runtime aborted the worker with RT005 on every request. `hw.detect()` would have shown invented Mac defaults instead (F2.8a on the tests branch). RAM and free disk now come from `std.sys`. Measured: those functions return WHOLE GIGABYTES as integers whatever their interface says, and the page had printed free disk with `str.fromf64`, as 7.9e-323. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/models/test_ollama_offline.tk` (3 assertions, against port 59431; the old module SIGSEGVs) and `tests/unit/browser/test_installer_page.tk`. `/installer` answers 200 in `scripts/smoke_serve.sh`. A caveat found while writing the test: `shared.reachability` binds the port to decide, so a port below 1024 always reads as "listening" to an unprivileged process. |
| F2.11 | S | **Done** — 2026-09-25 | **The reachability probe answered "down" for loke while loke was listening** — Found 2026-09-25. `shared.reachability.localserviceup` decided by BINDING the port (`net.portavailable`). Measured: it answered "free" for 11430 while loke listened there, because toke's server binds the wildcard address with `SO_REUSEPORT`, so a second bind on loopback succeeds. Every toke and ooke server does this, so moke believed loke was always down. It worked for Ollama only because Ollama does not set that option. **Fixed:** a "free" answer is confirmed by a real TCP connect (`connects`, through `nc -z`, since `std.net` has no connect and `net.listen` segfaults, T-49). **Evidence:** `tests/unit/shared/test_reachability_connect.tk`, whose listener assertion failed under mutation, and `scripts/smoke_e2e.sh`. **Caveat, still open:** a port below 1024 always reads as in use to an unprivileged process. |

## Epic F3: Privacy & Anonymisation Pipeline

*Build the multi-layer defence-in-depth system that detects PII, replaces it with reversible placeholders, and restores originals in responses. All implemented in toke on ooke.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| F3.1 | M | **Done** | Regex PII detector in toke (emails, phones, SSNs, credit cards, IPs, AU TFNs/ABNs — 10MB/s target, zero external deps) **Re-verified 2026-09-24 (RV1.5).** The detection half stands. Emails, phones, SSNs, cards, IPs, TFNs and ABNs each have assertions against the real module in `tests/unit/privacy/test_regex_detector.tk` (44 assertions), `test_regex.tk`, `test_regex_spans.tk` and `test_patterns.tk`. **The "10MB/s target" is measured and missed (F3.1a, 2026-09-24).** This Done covers detection, not throughput. See `docs/metrics-baseline.md` for the figure, and F3.1b for the quadratic cost behind it. |
| F3.1a | S | **Done** — 2026-09-24 | **Measure the regex detector's throughput against F3.1's 10MB/s target** — Filed 2026-09-24 by RV1.5. F3.1 has been **Done** with this target since it was written, and nothing has ever timed the detector. Run `core.privacy.regex` over a fixed synthetic corpus with a known PII density, at 1MB and 10MB, with the first run discarded as warm-up and N runs reported as a median and a range (VM1.3's method). Publish the result only in `docs/metrics-baseline.md`, labelled with the toke commit it was built against (X4.8). Either result is useful. Missing the target is a finding, not a failure of the story<br><br>**Done 2026-09-24. The target is missed.** Measured with `benchmarks/regex/run.py` (a new harness around `benchmarks/regex/bench.tk`, which times `core.privacy.regex.detect`) at toke `fedd48d`, 6 fresh-process runs per size with the first discarded. At 1 MB the median is roughly a twentieth of the target, and throughput falls as input grows. 10 MB never completes: all three attempts were killed by the OS. The figures, host, density and caveats are published only in `docs/metrics-baseline.md` ("Regex detector throughput"), and are not restated here. The cause is filed as F3.1b. |
| F3.1b | M | **Done** — 2026-09-27 | **The regex detector's time and memory grow with the square of the input, so a large prompt kills the process** — Filed 2026-09-24 by F3.1a. `docs/metrics-baseline.md` records peak RSS rising about ×3.7 for each doubling of input (141 MB at 0.25 MB, over 7 GB at 2 MB), and a 10 MB input is killed by the OS. In a single process, repeated 1 MB calls slow from 1.9 s to 7.3 s, because memory is not released between calls. The server is one long-lived process, so this reaches it. That is an availability failure and not a fail-open: a killed worker forwards nothing. The suspected cause is not yet verified. In `rundetection`, every match runs `str.substr(text;cursor;textlen)` to locate its span, which copies the rest of the text once per match, and `ph.applytotext` may repeat the pattern. Fix it and re-measure with `benchmarks/regex/run.py`. Acceptance: peak RSS grows linearly across 0.25 to 2 MB, and a 10 MB run completes.<br><br>**Done 2026-09-27.** The suspected cause was half the story. There were two allocations growing with matches × text length, neither ever freed. (1) The span search copied the remainder of the text per match; it now searches a window that grows fourfold. (2) `ph.applytotext` ran a global `str.replace` per ENTITY, so each repeat of a value copied the whole text and replaced nothing. Each distinct value is now replaced once, still globally, so no occurrence is missed. Fixing (1) alone halved memory and left it quadratic (82, 288 and 1 052 MB). A first attempt, an in-place byte search, was correct and 130× slower, because `str.charat` calls `strlen` per read (filed as T-55). **Measured** (`docs/metrics-baseline.md`, 2026-09-27, toke `0b0bc4e`, loke `0d29b5e`, VM1.3 method): peak RSS 40, 72, 138 and 276 MB at 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 MB, down from 141, 519, 1 971 and 7 185, so linear across that range. 10 MB completes in 15.9 s at 1.67 GB. Detections are identical to the old build at every size. **Both acceptance criteria are met.** **Still true:** time is superlinear (T-55), and 0.63 to 1.84 MB/s is far below F3.1's 10MB/s. `tests/unit/privacy` gains assertions that a repeated value is replaced at every occurrence, and that the window search finds a match past its first window. With the dedupe guard broken, six privacy suites fail. |

X7.6 made it assert the entity types each case declares, both ways. <br><br>**Status detail:** the harness runs over the built binary's request path; the CLI and Anthropic routes are not covered, and its guardian assertion fails on a product defect (F3.9a).<br><br>**Partial 2026-10-01 (W48).** The end-to-end harness now exists over the REAL request path: `scripts/smoke_privacy_harness.sh` (driver `scripts/lib/privacy_harness.py`), in the quality gate's Tests step after `smoke_e2e.sh`. Each detector type is exercised with one known-detected value; this is not a recall measurement (that is `test_detection_recall.tk`). |
| F3.9a | M | **Done** — 2026-10-01 | **The guardian system prompt never reaches the model on `POST /api/pipeline`** — Filed 2026-10-01 by F3.9. `core.privacy.pipeline.run` builds `finalsystemprompt` (the guardian, `core.privacy.guardian`) and the browser route does not send it. `page.api.pipeline.toollama` posts `{"model","prompt","stream"}` to `/api/generate` with no `system` field, and `toanthropic` builds its body from the caller's raw `system_prompt`, not from `run.finalsystemprompt`. Measured by `scripts/smoke_privacy_harness.sh`: the guardian reached the model in none of the dispatched cells (`docs/metrics-baseline.md`). The CLI paths (`cli.ask`, `cli.proxy`) do send it. ## Epic F3b: Configurable Multi-Layer Privacy Filters

*Extend the privacy pipeline to support multiple pluggable PII detection models — including the OpenAI Privacy Filter and other compatible token-classification models — with configurable layer ordering, per-layer confidence thresholds, and organisation-level trust policies. Users and organisations can compose their own defence-in-depth stack by choosing which filters run, in what order, and what to do when layers disagree.*

**Context:** The existing privacy pipeline (F3) uses regex (F3.1), local SLM NER (F3.2/F3.3), and Presidio (F3.4) as detection layers, orchestrated by the pipeline orchestrator (F3.6). This epic generalises the layer concept so that any compatible token-classification model — starting with [OpenAI Privacy Filter](https://huggingface.co/openai/privacy-filter) (Apache 2.0, 1.5B params, 50M active, runs on laptop, 128K context, 8 PII entity types, BIOES span decoding) — can be added as a detection layer alongside existing detectors. The key design goal is **composability**: organisations with strict compliance requirements can stack multiple independent models and require consensus before data leaves the device.

**Architectural principle:** Each privacy filter layer implements a common interface (`detect(text:str):@$piientity`). The pipeline orchestrator already supports layer sequencing and conflict resolution (F3.6). This epic adds: a filter registry, a layer configuration schema, trust/priority ordering, consensus policies, and the first external model integration (OpenAI Privacy Filter).

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|

Create a filter registry (`$filterregistry`) where layers are registered at startup. Migrate existing detectors (regex F3.1, NER F3.2/F3.3, Presidio F3.4) to implement this interface without changing their behaviour. Registry supports `register`, `list`, `get`, `remove`. The read is read-only, and `settings.json` already set this precedent, but a test must not depend on a person's configuration. Every test path helper resolves through `$HOME` (`std.homedir()`, `proc.homedir()`, `os.getenv("HOME")`; measured in the pinned runtime, all three read `getenv("HOME")`), so under the old runner about sixty tests made their scratch directories inside the developer's own `~/.loke` (`test-mapping-deletion`, `test-palace-wings`, `test-kill-switch` and the rest), and anything loading the user's `config.toml`, `settings.json`, `loke.db`, log or memory palace used the real one. **Built.** (1) `scripts/run_tests.sh` runs every test binary under its own fresh, empty `HOME` (`$BUILDDIR/home/<test>`, removed and recreated before each run), so those directories move with it and no test lost coverage; `scripts/build_test.sh` does the same. (2) A guard, `scripts/lib/realhome_guard.c`, injected into every test binary with `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, records each libc filesystem call (open, fopen in both exported names, stat, lstat, access, opendir, mkdir, unlink, rename, realpath and their `at` forms) whose path is the real `~/.loke` or under it, a read as much as a write. A test that touched it is reported `REAL_HOME` with the paths and fails the run whatever its own assertions said; this also catches a hardcoded absolute path, which a `HOME` override alone would not. Before trusting its silence the runner proves it is live with a probe that `stat`s a name that does not exist under the real `~/.loke`, and refuses to run if the probe went unrecorded. **Evidence.** Full suite under the new runner: 190 pass, 0 fail, 190 binaries guarded, no `REAL_HOME`. **Mutants:** (a) the runner with `HOME` set back to the real home: a test calling the production `shared.config.loaded()` fails `REAL_HOME` with `access ~/.loke/config.toml`, and the same test passes under the real runner; (b) a test that checks `~/.loke/config.toml` by absolute path fails `REAL_HOME` under the real runner. **Keychain (X8.7, unchanged by decision):** `tests/unit/storage/test_keychain.tk`, `tests/integration/test_keychain_e2e.tk` and `tests/test_keychain_settings.tk` still write and delete their own items in the real login keychain. Measured: the Security framework finds the keychain through `$HOME/Library/Keychains`, and under an empty `HOME` `test_keychain_e2e` blocked indefinitely. Those three, and only those, get a link to the real `Library/Keychains` in their throwaway `HOME`; their `~/.loke` is still throwaway and the guard still applies. **Not done:** (1) the guard sees paths passed to libc only: keychain traffic (securityd IPC) and anything a test reaches through a child process that strips `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` (system binaries under SIP, e.g. `/bin/sh`) are invisible to it; such a child still inherits the throwaway `HOME`. (2) Only the toke test runners are covered; the smokes already used a throwaway `HOME`, and the moke JavaScript tests were not examined. (3) Production paths are still built from `$HOME` rather than injected; the isolation is the runner's, not the modules'. (4) Directories earlier runs left in the real `~/.loke` (`test-*`) were not removed: that would be a write to the user's data, so it is left to the user. |

## Epic F6: Storage & Audit Layer

*Persistent encrypted local storage for conversations, audit trails, PII mappings, configuration, and cache. Implemented in toke using SQLite + SQLCipher via ooke native bindings.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| F6.1 | L | **Done** | SQLite database schema (SQLCipher via ooke native bindings, WAL mode, foreign keys, numbered migrations with checksum verification, typed data access layer with parameterised queries) `[R3.1, R3.2, R3.6, R3.7]` |
| F6.2 | L | **Done** | Audit trail system (append-only, hash chain, tamper detection, export, SIEM forwarding; metadata only — never stores prompt/response content) `[R3.5, R4.7]` |
| F6.3 | M | **Done** | Vector store for semantic operations (via ooke native bindings — replaces LanceDB; prompt cache, routing examples) |
| F6.4 | L | **Done** | Secure ephemeral storage (mlock equivalent via ooke, secure wipe, auto-expiry, no disk serialisation) |
| F6.5 | M | **Done** | Database backup and restore (consistent snapshot via SQLite VACUUM INTO, timestamped naming, configurable retention, restore with validation) `[R3.8, R8.5]` — *spec remains valid* |
| F6.6 | M | **Done** | Persistent sync queue (enqueue/dequeue with retry and exponential backoff, survives restarts — implemented in toke) `[R3.4, R8.7]` — *spec remains valid* |
| F6.7 | M | **Done** | Namespaced settings store (typed key-value: string, number, boolean, JSON; `loke.*` prefix + application prefix; get/set/list API — implemented in toke) `[R3.3]` — *spec remains valid* |
| F6.8 | S | **Done** — 2026-09-24 | **A migration that failed was recorded as applied, and never retried** — Found 2026-09-24. A worker flagged it and it was confirmed by reading. In `core.storage.db.runmigrations`, each `mt db.exec(...) { $ok:v 1; $err:e $err(...) }` was a STATEMENT, so its value, the error included, was discarded. A migration whose SQL failed was then inserted into `schema_migrations` as applied. Every later migration ran against a schema missing its predecessor, and nothing reported it. The same applied to creating `schema_migrations` itself. **Fixed:** `applymigrations` stops at the first failure, does not record it, logs at ERROR naming the migration, and answers the failed version. `openstore` logs how many migrations are pending (`pendingmigrations`). That log line is the visible signal, because `runmigrations`'s own `$err` reaches a `!$lokeerr` match, which T-18 reads as `$ok` (LS1.1j). **Evidence:** six assertions in `tests/unit/storage/test_db.tk` using test-only versions 9001 to 9003: an invalid migration followed by a valid one. The failed version is reported, it is not recorded, nothing after it runs, both stay pending, and a valid one applies and is recorded. With the stop-on-failure branch disabled, 4 of them failed. |

## Epic F8: Companion Device Support

*Extend local compute to nearby high-power devices over secure direct connections. Implemented in toke on ooke.*

> **F8.1–F8.4 compile now, and they still cannot work.** My earlier note here said `std.mdns` and `std.tls` declare types whose names toke cannot write, so these were blocked upstream. **That was wrong** — the compiler resolves those functions from its builtin table regardless of the `.tki`, and all four stories' modules now compile. The real position is worse for the feature: **every function in `std.tls` and `std.mdns` is a stub that ignores its arguments and returns 0** (T-11 in [`docs/upstream/toke-issues.md`](upstream/toke-issues.md)). There is no TLS and no mDNS on this toolchain.<br><br>Two specifics matter for F8.2's claim. `tls.tlsconfig` now takes `(cert, key)` only: the peer certificate and verify-peer flag that **are** the mutual-authentication half have nowhere to go, so "TLS 1.3 mutual auth" is not untested — it cannot be expressed through this API. And `tls.genselfsigned` takes a common name, so the 3650-day validity loke asked for is passed to nothing. `companion/channel.tk` therefore fails closed and logs why, rather than returning a zero handle a caller would treat as an encrypted socket. **F8.1 and F8.2 move from Done to reopened; F8.3 and F8.4 stay in RV1 for re-verification** since they use REST and do not depend on these primitives.

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| F8.1 | L | **Reopened** | Companion device discovery and pairing (mDNS via ooke, confirmation codes, security checks) |
| F8.2 | L | **Reopened** | Secure communication channel (TLS 1.3 mutual auth, certificate pinning, heartbeat — via ooke TLS primitives) |
| F8.3 | XL | **Reopened** — no importer, so no router integration and no privacy pipeline | Remote model execution (companion Ollama/Exo via REST, router integration, privacy pipeline applied) **Reopened 2026-09-24 (RV1.6).** `core.companion.executor` compiles and **nothing imports it**: a grep of `packages`, `src` and `tests` for an `i=…:core.companion` import finds none outside the companion directory itself. So the row's "router integration" and "privacy pipeline applied" are both false, because no request can reach this code. The exposure is nil for the same reason. It needs fixing before anything calls it: `executeconn` sends `req.prompt` as given, so a future caller that forgot to anonymise first would send raw text to the companion. `parseremoteresponse` also returns `ok:true` whatever it parses, so a malformed or error reply reads as success with empty text. No test exercises any of it. |
| F8.4 | L | **Reopened** — no importer; no cluster monitoring surface exists | Exo distributed inference integration (GPL-3.0 boundary maintained — REST API only, cluster monitoring) **Reopened 2026-09-24 (RV1.6).** `core.companion.exo` has **no importers**, found by the same grep as F8.3, so nothing monitors a cluster and nothing routes to Exo. The GPL boundary claim does hold, trivially: the module speaks only REST, and nothing links Exo. That is the one part of this row that is true. No test exercises it. |

*Infrastructure and extension points that make loke a platform applications can build on. These epics enable third-party applications to use loke's privacy, routing, and storage capabilities without forking the core.*

# ACCOUNTABLE AI SYSTEMS LAYER

*Every AI capability executes within accountability controls. This layer sits between user intent and AI services, making every interaction governed, risk-classified, auditable, and owned. The goal is not to control the model — it's to control the system in which the model operates.*

## Epic G1: AI Governance Gateway

*Every AI request — browser mode, terminal mode, MCP tool call, or agent action — passes through a single governance gateway that enforces policy, logs decisions, and ensures accountability before anything executes.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| G1.1 | XL | **Done** | Governance gateway implementation (single mandatory entry point for all AI interactions; executes in order: authenticate → classify risk → check policy → filter data → log → route; `gateway.submit(request)` → `GatewayDecision`; < 100ms overhead; hot-reloadable config; F3/F4/F5 plug in as stages) |
| G1.2 | L | **Done** | Use case registry (built-in use cases: chat-completion, code-generation, code-review, summarisation, data-analysis, translation, classification, agent-task, mcp-tool-call; custom use case registration; each stores id, name, risk_level, purpose, approved_models, required_controls, owner; `loke use-cases list/add`) |
| G1.3 | L | **Done** | Risk classification and control gates (three tiers: Low → logging + guardrails + anonymisation; Medium + human-visible preview + cost confirmation; High + mandatory approval + explainability trace + enhanced audit; dynamic escalation when data sensitivity exceeds use case default; colour-coded indicator on every request) |
| G1.4 | M | **Done** | Accountability and ownership registry (business/technical/risk owner per use case; defaults to user for individual installs; owner metadata on every audit event; no use case active without assigned owner; `loke owners list`; changes logged) |
| G1.5 | M | **Done** | AI justification requirement (new use case registration requires: purpose, why AI vs simpler alternative, expected value, identified risks; built-in justifications pre-written; suggest simpler paths when AI is unnecessary; enterprise sign-off workflow) |
| G1.6 | M | **Partial** — 2026-10-06: every external call path checks the switch, fail closed; enterprise remote trigger not built | Kill switch and fallback mode (global: `loke kill-switch on` stops all external AI calls; per-provider, per-use-case, per-agent; graceful fallback messaging; persisted across restarts; audit trail; enterprise remote trigger via policy push)<br><br>**Reopened 2026-09-26 by T10.1.** The Done marker was false for part of the row. Until T10.1 there was no per-provider scope at all; it now exists and is enforced before dispatch. Per-use-case and per-agent scope still do not exist (`isblocked` takes a use case and ignores it), and no enterprise remote trigger was checked. What is true: the global switch blocks every request (403), fails closed on an unreadable store, persists in settings across restarts, and is audited.<br><br>**Per-use-case and per-agent scope, 2026-09-28.** `core.governance.killswitch` gains `engageusecase`/`releaseusecase`/`isusecaseblocked` and `engageagent`/`releaseagent`/`isagentblocked`, one flag each in the settings table beside the global and provider flags, so they persist across restarts. The use cases accepted are the ones a request path passes, which today is only `browser-chat` (`page.api.pipeline`); any other id, including the ids in `core.governance.usecases`' registry that nothing on a request path consults, is refused so that a switch cannot report a use case blocked while nothing refuses it. Agent ids are checked for shape (1-64 of `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`). Fail closed as the global switch does: no store, or a settings table that cannot be read, means blocked (`set.getboolor` returned "not engaged" on a read error, so the scoped reads do not use it). `isblocked(store;provider;usecase)` now honours its use case, and `blockedscope`/`refusalmessage` name the switch that refused. Every engage and release, global and provider included, writes an `audit_log` row (`kill_switch_engaged`/`kill_switch_released`, scope and target in `correlation_id`). **Wired:** `page.api.pipeline` refuses a switched-off `browser-chat` with 403 before the body is read or scanned, so not even the local NER model is asked, and audits it as `kill_switch_refused`; its provider check after routing also honours the use case. `core.agents.executor.execute` takes the store in `$executorconfig` and refuses a switched-off agent (or any agent while the global switch is engaged or unreadable) before building or scanning its prompt, recording a sandbox violation and an audit row. **CLI:** `loke kill-switch <on\|off> [--use-case <id> \| --agent <id> \| --provider <name>]` and `loke kill-switch status` write the running server's `loke.db`, so a change applies on the next request with no restart. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/governance/test_kill_switch.tk` (+38 assertions: a use case blocks only that use case; an agent only that agent; both survive a reopened store; a renamed-away settings table and a missing store both block; engage, release and refusal audit rows), `tests/unit/agents/test_executor_killswitch.tk` (new, 10: a switched-off agent is not run, another agent is not refused by the switch, no store refuses all, release restores), `tests/unit/cli/test_commands.tk` (+12, parsing). Six mutants, each killed: use-case flag ignored (6 assertions fail), scoped read fails open (2), agent flag ignored (3 + 4 in the executor test), audit rows not written (5 + 1), executor not consulting the switch (5), `isblocked` ignoring the use case (4). `scripts/smoke_e2e.sh` engages the switch through the real CLI binary against the running server, then judges the 403 body over HTTP (`"kill_switch_scope":"use_case"` and the message naming `browser-chat`), asserts neither the model nor the NER layer received anything and that the engaged and refused audit rows exist, then releases it and gets a 200. **Not done:** (1) enterprise remote trigger via policy push: nothing in `core.policy` engages a switch (`core.governance.external.dispatchkillswitch` only notifies outward). (2) The per-agent switch guards no live traffic yet: `core.agents.executor.execute` has no production caller, because agent runs are stubbed. (3) Only `browser-chat` is a use case, because it is the only one any path passes; the gateway's use-case registry is not on the request path.<br><br>**Every path, 2026-10-06.** Each path that asks a model to answer was checked for the switch. *Already checked:* the browser `/api/pipeline` (global ahead of the scan, then per hop: provider and `browser-chat`), the no-custody dispatch (`core.nocustody.dispatch.attempt`, at its entry; untested until now). *Gaps fixed:* (a) `loke ask` checked no switch (F5.3). `core.router.fallback.dispatchchain` now takes the store and a use case and asks `ks.isblocked` for every hop after the routing gate and before the send; `loke ask` opens `loke.db` at `config.datadir` and passes `cli-ask`, so a store that cannot be opened refuses every hop. (b) The CLI proxy (`cli.proxy.handlerequest`) checked none; it now asks first, before the request is read or scanned, with `cli-proxy`, and answers `{"error":"kill_switch",...}`. `loke proxy` is not wired to a CLI command, so this path is compiled and tested but not reachable from the binary. (c) **An unreadable switch read as off:** the global and provider flags were read with `set.getboolor`, whose default on a read error is "not engaged". A request was still refused at its send, because the use-case read (`flagfailclosed`) fails closed, but the browser's global guard ahead of the scan read the switch as off, so the body was scanned (the local NER model asked) before the refusal, and `blockedscope` named the wrong switch. `ks.globalblocked` (engaged, no store, or unreadable) is now that guard and the global read in `blockedscope`, and the provider flag is read fail closed too, so no scope depends on another to fail closed.`cli-ask`, `cli-proxy` and `no-custody` are registered use cases, so each can be switched off on its own. *No path to gate:* the MCP broker calls loopback upstreams only and refuses any other (`mcpbroker.proxy.proxysendrequest`), the toke MCP server makes no outbound call, and `core.mcp.client` has no importer; `browser.extensions.core` builds a dispatcher and never dispatches; `loke bench` refuses cloud models. **Decision for the user — moke's `/api/proxy` is left ungated.** It fetches data sources the Connections page names (`moke.proxy.fetch`), under the `MOKE_PROXY_ALLOW` allowlist, which is empty by default. It is an outbound call, but not an AI call: it carries no prompt and asks no model, so it is outside "stops all external AI calls" as this row words it. If the switch is meant to stop all egress, it should be gated too; moke has no handle on `loke.db` today, so that would be its own change. **Evidence:** `tests/integration/test_kill_switch_paths.tk` (new, 29 assertions) drives each path's production module against a `scripts/lib/http_recorder.py` Ollama and judges the count of POSTs that arrived: for `loke ask`, the proxy, no-custody and a browser hop, the control (switch released) reaches the stand-in, and the global switch, the provider's switch and the path's use-case switch each let nothing arrive; a store of 0 and a settings table renamed away (so every read fails) make every path send nothing and refuse, with a readable control after. **Mutants** (each alone; file kept outside the tree, restored, verified with `cmp`): (1) `loke ask`: the per-hop check in `dispatchchain` made `blocked=false` fails 8 of `test_kill_switch_paths.tk`, first "LOKE ASK SENDS NOTHING WITH THE GLOBAL KILL SWITCH ON", then the provider, the `cli-ask` use case, no store and the unreadable table. (2) The CLI proxy's check made `if(false)` fails 6, first "THE PROXY SENDS NOTHING WITH THE GLOBAL KILL SWITCH ON" and its refusal body. (3) The browser hop's check in `hoprefusal` made `if(false)` fails 3 in `test_kill_switch_paths.tk` ("A BROWSER HOP SENDS NOTHING WITH THE GLOBAL KILL SWITCH ON, and the reply is 403") and 3 in `test_browser_fallback.tk`. (4) The no-custody check made `if(false)` fails 4, first "THE NO-CUSTODY DISPATCH SENDS NOTHING WITH THE GLOBAL KILL SWITCH ON, and refuses with 403". (5) The unreadable switch failing open again (`globalblocked` without `flagfailclosed`, the provider read back on `set.getboolor`) fails 2: "AN UNREADABLE GLOBAL FLAG BLOCKS, where isengaged reads it as off" and "and each refuses" (the browser guard). It does NOT fail "no path sends anything", because the use-case read still refuses at the send, which is what (c) above says. The unmutated control passed all eight test files. **Not done:** (1) enterprise remote trigger via policy push, as before. (2) The per-agent switch still guards no live traffic. (3) moke's `/api/proxy`, above, pending the user's decision. |

| AG1.9 | S | **Done** — 2026-09-25 | **Agent lookup cannot say "not found", and duplicate ids are accepted** — Found 2026-09-24 closing T12.3. `core.agents.registry.find` returns an `$agentdef` through `i64!$lokeerr`, so its three callers — `scheduler.triggermanual`, `overnight` (job loop) and `agents.pipeline` (step loop) — take the first arm whatever happened (T-18): an unknown agent name is treated as found, and `find` itself loops `i>count` one past the end with `str.arrayget`. `get(reg;id)` (empty id when absent) and `has` now exist and are tested; move the three callers onto them. Separately, `register` accepts a second agent with an id already registered, and its `$err` arms (empty name, empty prompt) are unobservable for the same reason — return the registry unchanged plus a predicate, as `enable`/`disable` do. **Done 2026-09-25.** All three callers now ask `reg.has` first. `agents.pipeline` and `overnight` use it for the step and job check, and `scheduler.triggermanual` refuses an unknown id before it can run anything. `overnight.runbatch` and `pipeline.runpipeline` declared the registry as `i64`, a parameter that shadowed the module alias; both now take `$agentregistry`. Neither has a caller. `register` refuses a duplicate id, an empty name and an empty prompt by returning the registry UNCHANGED, which callers can observe, and logs why; two of its old error arms were not even wrapped in `$err`. Found on the way: `runpipeline` had never been called, and its first call died with RT005 nil dereference, because it read steps through the type-erasing `t.arrayget` (F10.22). It now uses a typed `.get`. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/agents/test_registry.tk` asserts that a duplicate is refused with the original untouched, that a nameless agent is refused, and that a two-step pipeline with an unknown agent is not ok, runs the known step and reports the unknown one as not found. With the old lookup and `register` restored, it failed. |
| AG1.10 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-26 | **The agent sandbox cannot decide a permission correctly, and nothing uses it** — Found 2026-09-25 closing LS1.1t. `core.agents.sandbox.checkpermission` returns `i64`, and both callers use it as a `bool`. `sandboxreadfile` and `sandboxhttpget` build their permission as a bare sum variant in value position (`$readfile(path)`), which T-13 records as producing a value that crashes. Violations were never recorded (its own comment). The module has no importer, so no agent is sandboxed today. Before any agent runs untrusted work: retype `checkpermission` to `bool`, build permissions through a constructor, thread the violation log back to the caller, and test a granted read, a refused read and a path outside the grant.<br><br>**Done 2026-09-26.** `checkpermission` takes a `$agentpermission` and returns `bool`, and reads the grants typed rather than through `str.arrayget`. Permissions are built by `readpermission`, `writepermission`, `toolpermission`, `getpermission` and `modelpermission`, never as bare variants. `readfile` and `httpget` return a `$sandboxstep` that carries the sandbox, so a refusal's violation reaches the caller. They replace the `str!$lokeerr` forms, which no caller could discriminate (T-18). **Also fixed, found while doing it:** grants were matched with `str.contains`. Paths now match at a directory boundary and any `..` segment is refused. URLs match at a `/`, `?` or `#` boundary. `core.agents.executor` built its model permission with field syntax and declared three functions `i64` that return `$sandboxresult`; both are corrected. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/agents/test_sandbox.tk` has 24 assertions. They cover a granted read that returns the file, a refused read that does not read it and records one violation, a traversal read and a refused fetch recorded as the second and third, and the prefix and host-confusion cases. It fails 8 with the old `str.contains` matching restored. **Still true:** `core.agents.executor` has no importer, so no agent is sandboxed at run time yet. A granted fetch of a dead endpoint is unsafe to read, because `http.get` returns `$ok` with a nil body (T-15). |

# MEMORY PALACE AND AAAK SHORTHAND

*Persistent cross-session memory organised into a navigable palace structure, with AAAK shorthand for efficient context loading. Adapted from the MemPalace architecture (MIT, github.com/milla-jovovich/mempalace) for local-first use. All memory stays on-device, passes through the privacy pipeline, and integrates with governance and audit.*

## Epic M2: AAAK Shorthand Integration

*AAAK is compressed English shorthand readable by any LLM without a decoder — not a programming language, not a binary format. Complementary to TOON (F4.1, structured data) and toke (prompt syntax): AAAK specifically optimises natural-language memory and context loading.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| M1.8 | L | **Done** — 2026-09-24 | **The memory palace and the store are two databases, and `std.db` has one connection** — Found 2026-09-23 by a de-stubbed test. `core.storage.db.openstore` opens `datadir/loke.db`; `core.memory.palace.openpalace` opens `datadir/memory.db`. `std.db` keeps a **single global connection** (`g_db`, `src/stdlib/db.c:10`) and `conn_db` resolves only conn_id 0, so `db.open`'s returned handle selects nothing and **every query from both subsystems goes to whichever database was opened last** — filed upstream as T-30. `audit_log` does not exist in `memory.db` and `memory_drawers` does not exist in `loke.db`, so the loser's queries fail **silently**, because `rowi64`/`rowstr` map a failed read to `0`/`""`. It was invisible until `tests/unit/memory/test_palace_drawers.tk` was de-stubbed and started asserting the tables exist. Three routes, and the choice is architectural rather than mechanical: put the memory tables in `loke.db` and drop the second file (simplest, and a single file is one thing to encrypt and one thing to delete — see X8.2/X8.4); keep two files and re-open the right one before every operation (correct but fragile, and it serialises); or wait for T-30 and pass the handle. **Do not "fix" it by reordering the opens** — that makes the working case depend on call order, which is the defect. Sibling of M1.7, which is the four memory tables no migration creates at all **Update 2026-09-24:** the route was chosen and the code landed in `3ead30d` (M1.7). The palace opens `loke.db` and the memory tables come from migrations, so this is route one. `tests/unit/memory/test_palace_one_db.tk` opens the store, then `palace.open` on the same datadir. It asserts that `audit_log` and `settings` are still visible, that `memory_drawers` is in the same database, and that no `memory.db` is created. It passes, 7 of 7 memory tests. A probe confirmed the assertion discriminates: a second `db.open` on `memory.db` after `openstore` makes `tableexists("audit_log")` false.<br><br>**Status detail — done 2026-09-24.** Seen red against the old behaviour: with `palace.open` mutated back to `str.concat(datadir;"/memory.db")` and the tree rebuilt, `tests/unit/memory/test_palace_one_db.tk` failed 3 assertions (`audit_log` not visible after `palace.open`, `settings` not visible, a `memory.db` created). Restored, rebuilt, green. |

| X4.6 | S | **Done** | **A sweep commit must be provably mechanical** — `scripts/verify_held_changes.py` already checks that held toke changes are an equality-only substitution, it existed when `09b0a67` landed, and it correctly flags a line-count change as *"not a substitution"*. But it guards the **working tree**, so once a change is committed it has nothing to compare against — and nothing checks that a commit *described* as a mechanical sweep actually was one. That gap cost 161 lines of working request-path wiring (GA1.10). Add a pre-push check: for a commit touching more than N files whose message names a mechanical migration, any file with a net line delta beyond a small threshold must be listed explicitly in the message. ## Epic X4a: Module-Aware API Handler Compilation

*loke's API handlers (`pages/api/*.tk`) are toke source files that import modules from the core engine (`core.privacy.pipeline`, `core.router`, `shared.types`, etc.). Currently ooke compiles page templates but falls through to a static echo for API handlers because the toke compiler cannot resolve cross-module imports at serve time. This means all API endpoints (`/api/pipeline`, `/api/health`, `/api/models`, etc.) return either ooke's default response or echo the request body — no loke business logic executes.*

**Root cause:** When ooke serves an API route backed by a `.tk` handler, it needs to compile that handler into a callable function. The handler imports other modules via `i=alias:module.path;`, but the compiler has no module search path configured — it can only compile single-file programs. The same gap blocks the test suite (X4b.3).

**Impact:** loke and moke build and serve static pages correctly, but every API call that requires the privacy pipeline, router, model registry, governance gateway, or any core module returns a no-op response. The product is visually complete but functionally inert.

**Dependency:** This requires changes in both toke (module search path, multi-file compilation) and ooke (passing module roots to the compiler when compiling handlers). The `--emit-deps` standalone build pipeline works for single-file programs (proven by the test suite) but not for files with cross-module imports.

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| X4a.1 | XL | **Done** | **toke: multi-file module resolution** — Add a `--module-path <dir>` flag (repeatable) to toke that tells the compiler where to search for imported modules. When compiling `source.tk` that contains `i=alias:module.path;`, the compiler searches each `--module-path` directory for a file whose `m=` declaration matches `module.path`. Resolves the module's type interface (generates `.tki` if needed) so the importing file can type-check. At link time, compiles all transitively imported modules and links them together. This is the critical missing piece — without it, no multi-file toke program can compile. |
| X4a.2 | L | **Done** | **ooke: pass module paths when compiling handlers** — When ooke compiles an API handler `.tk` file, pass the project's source directories as `--module-path` arguments to toke. For loke, this means: `--module-path packages/core/src --module-path packages/shared/src --module-path packages/browser/src --module-path src`. Read module paths from `ooke.toml` config (new `[build] module_paths = [...]` field). Handlers should compile with full access to the project's module graph. |
| X4a.3 | L | **Done** | **Verify loke API handlers compile and execute** — Once X4a.1 and X4a.2 are complete, verify that all loke API handlers compile with module resolution and return correct responses: `/api/health` (returns loke version, Ollama status, port), `/api/pipeline` (runs privacy pipeline on input text, returns anonymised output), `/api/models` (returns available model list from Ollama), `/api/settings` (returns current config). Test from moke's chat interface — a prompt should flow through the full pipeline and return an LLM response. **Re-verified 2026-09-24 (RV1.2): this was FALSE until today, and it is true now.** The handlers compiled, but with the server running, `/api/health`, `/api/models` and `/api/pipeline` each killed the worker process on their first request. The pages `/privacy`, `/savings` and `/pipeline` did the same. The cause was F10.36: ooke objects compiled by an older toke clobbered the runtime's thread-local error flag. Fixed there. Evidence now: `scripts/smoke_serve.sh` makes a real request to every route and fails on a dropped connection. It is in `quality-gate.sh`'s test step, and it went red against the old objects before it was trusted. |
| X4a.4 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-25 | **Verify moke API handlers compile and execute** — Verify moke's API handlers: `/api/health` (proxies to loke health), `/api/feedback` (stores feedback), `/api/memory` (searches memory palace), `/api/datasets` (lists uploaded datasets), `/api/upload` (processes CSV upload), `/api/pipeline` (proxies pipeline call through loke). **Reopened 2026-09-24 (RV1.2).** The moke tree has 0 compile errors, but six objects still fail IR assembly (MK21.16), so there is no moke binary. A handler cannot "execute and return correct responses" from a server that cannot be built. This row is also the cited evidence for retiring BUG-7, so that retirement no longer has evidence either. The BUG-7 line in the BG1 migration table is annotated to match. **Done 2026-09-25, re-verified against the running server.** moke links (MK21.16). `scripts/smoke_serve_moke.sh` requests 11 pages and loads all 17 datasets through `/api/datasets`, and it is in the gate. Running it the first time fixed `/` and `/chat`, which returned null (LS1.1u). |

## Epic X4a.5: Core Module Semantic Fixes

*With toke v3 syntax migration complete (562/562 files) and module-aware compilation working (X4a.1–X4a.2), 94 of 168 core modules still fail semantic checks. These are code-level issues — undeclared identifiers, missing imports, type mismatches, and mutability errors — that prevent `.tki` interface generation and block the full module dependency graph from resolving.*

**Root cause:** The v3 migration fixed syntax but not semantics. Many modules reference sum type variants, stdlib functions, or types without proper imports or declarations. Some use `i64` where `i32`/`u32` is expected. Some assign to immutable bindings.

## Epic X4a.7: CORS Architecture Resolution

*Cross-origin issues between moke (:11432) and loke (:11430) have been a recurring problem. The `ooke.toml` `corsorigins = "*"` setting works for preflight (OPTIONS) and actual requests when the Origin header is present, but the browser-side JS health polling still shows connectivity issues. This epic proposes an architectural change to eliminate CORS as a concern.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| X4a.7.1 | S | **Done** | **Audit current CORS state** — Document exactly where CORS is configured (ooke.toml, ooke http.c headers), what the browser sees (inspect Network tab), and whether the issue is CORS headers missing on specific routes or a different connectivity problem (e.g. moke's JS fetching wrong URL, health endpoint returning non-JSON). |
| X4a.7.2 | M | **Done** | **Auto-detect same-origin or cross-origin** — `base.tkt` probes `/api/health` as a relative path first. If it returns a valid loke response (has `d.loke` field), sets `window.LOKE_URL = ''` so all templates use relative paths (no CORS). If the probe fails, falls back to `CROSS_ORIGIN_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:11430'` for dev-mode cross-origin. All templates already use `window.LOKE_URL \|\| 'http://127.0.0.1:11430'` fallback. |
| X4a.7.3 | S | **Done** | **Both approaches work** — Same-origin works when loke serves moke (single port or reverse proxy). Cross-origin works in dev (moke:11432 → loke:11430) with ooke CORS headers. No code changes needed per deployment — auto-detection handles it. |
| X4a.7.4 | S | **Done** | **Verified implementation** — `probeAndResolve()` in base.tkt handles the decision at runtime. `corsorigins` kept in ooke.toml as a safety net for dev mode. Templates use `window.LOKE_URL + '/api/...'` which resolves to either relative or absolute paths. |

## Epic X4b: Archive Legacy Tests & Create New Test Suites

*The v3 migration converted all 562 source files to valid toke v3 syntax. The 170 existing test files (156 loke + 14 moke) were written against the pre-ooke architecture using patterns that no longer compile (v2 test framework references, unresolvable module imports, pre-migration assertion patterns). These tests need to be archived and replaced with clean test suites for loke and moke separately.*

**Blocker:** The toke compiler currently links `tk_web_glue.o` on every build, which requires ooke's db/collections C libraries. A standalone `--no-web-glue` compilation mode is needed in toke before any test binary can be produced. This is being addressed in the toke project. Once resolved, test files can compile to standalone binaries via `tkc --out <binary> <test.tk>`.

**Context:** `std.test` exists in toke's stdlib (`tk_test.c` / `tk_test.h`) and provides `test.assert(cond;msg)`, `test.assert_eq(a;b;msg)`, `test.assert_ne(a;b;msg)`. Test files should follow the convention `f=main():i64` returning 0 for all-pass, non-zero for failure count. The existing `.tkc.md` companion files (156 of them) document the intended test behaviour and can be used as specifications for rewriting.

| X4b.1 | S | **Done** | **Archive legacy loke test files** — Move the 156 existing test files from `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/`, and `tests/e2e/` into `_archived-tests/loke/`. Preserve directory structure. These files are syntactically valid v3 but cannot compile due to unresolvable module imports and broken test framework references. Keep the `.tkc.md` companion files alongside their test files — they document intended test behaviour and serve as specs for rewriting. Add a `_archived-tests/README.md` explaining the archive reason (v3 migration, test framework gap) and that companion files contain the canonical test specifications. |

Same approach: preserve structure, keep companion files, document the archive. The 3 test files we rewrote during migration (`feedback_test.tk`, `memory_test.tk`, `pipeline_panel_test.tk`) are placeholder stubs — archive them with the rest. |

# WRAPPER PROJECT SCOPE

*The following requirements from the platform requirements document are domain-specific or application-level concerns. They should be implemented in the application built on loke, not in loke itself. loke provides the extension points; the wrapper provides the implementation.*

| Requirement | Why it's wrapper scope | loke provides |
|---|---|---|
| **R8.3 — Calendar integration** (Microsoft Graph adapter, list/create/update/delete events, free/busy) | Domain-specific — not every loke application needs calendar. | P5.1 integration adapter interface + P5.2 OAuth 2.0 flow. Wrapper implements the calendar adapter. |
| **R8.4 — Conferencing integration** (Teams/Zoom meeting links, recordings, transcripts) | Domain-specific. | P5.1 adapter interface. Wrapper implements conferencing adapters. |
| **R9.2 — Multi-timezone display** (simultaneous timezone comparison) | Meeting-planning UX, not core to privacy/LLM proxy. | P4.3 locale-aware date/time formatting. Wrapper builds the multi-tz UI. |
| **R9.3 — Meeting planner** (timezone overlap grid, working hours, participant availability) | Productivity-app feature. | UTC storage (F6.1), Intl APIs (P4.3). Wrapper builds the planner. |
| **R9.4 — InterPlanet timezone provider** | Novelty/future-proof feature, not core. | P4.3 uses standard Intl.DateTimeFormat. Wrapper implements custom provider. |
| **R10.1–R10.3 — P2P metadata sync, sync status, conflict resolution** | Multi-user collaboration beyond loke's local-first single-user model. F8 companion devices cover compute offload, not data sync. | F8 companion device infrastructure (mDNS, TLS). Wrapper builds sync protocol and conflict resolution on top. |
| **R11.3 — Central notifications** (policy changes, announcements from central source) | Enterprise distribution concern. | P3.8 notification system. Wrapper pushes notifications from its central endpoint. |
| **R11.4 — Central authentication** (each install authenticates against configurable endpoint) | Enterprise deployment concern. | P1.3 middleware pipeline with pluggable auth. Wrapper implements the auth adapter. |
| **R14.3 — Enhancement request form** (structured feature request with use case, priority) | Application-level UX, not platform infrastructure. | A5.1 issue reporting form pattern. Wrapper extends with enhancement-specific fields. |

### Timezone note

loke stores all timestamps in UTC (F6.1) and uses `Intl` APIs for display formatting (P4.3). R9.1 (UTC throughout) and R9.5 (relative time) are covered by P4.3. The wrapper is responsible for any multi-timezone comparison UI, meeting planning, or custom timezone providers.

### Multi-user note

loke is local-first and single-user by design. The companion device support (F8) provides secure device-to-device communication for compute offload. If the wrapper needs multi-user data sync, it should build on F8's mDNS discovery and TLS channel, implementing its own sync protocol, conflict resolution, and metadata scope. loke's F6.6 sync queue provides the persistent outbound queue primitive.

# DEMO LAYER — moke

*moke is a data analysis demo application built on loke, demonstrating the extension API (P2.6–P2.8) and showing what a domain-specific application looks like. moke is a toke/ooke package at `/packages/moke/` that imports from `core.*` and adds its own pages, data, and pipeline stages without forking any loke source. It is the reference implementation of loke's extensibility pattern.*

*The original moke was a Node.js/Express prototype (`/moke/`) that proved the schema-first data protocol, local compute engine, dashboard generation, and Insight Lab concepts. The toke moke re-implements all DONE features from that prototype as a first-class ooke application.*

---

| MK6.5 | S | **Done** — 2026-09-27 | **Nine moke API handlers can never be reached** — Found 2026-09-27 by X7.2, probing the running moke. ooke's `scripts/gen_handlers.sh` registers exactly one `get` and one `post` per page file, which is its documented convention, and moke's handler registry is generated from it. So `pages/api/ml.tk`'s `postrun` and `postpropose`, `pages/api/mcp.tk`'s `gettools`, `postinvoke`, `getbroker`, `getmemory` and `postmemory`, and `pages/api/agents.tk`'s `postscan`, `postschema` and `getdiary` compile but have no route: a request answers 404 or 405. Nothing in the moke UI calls them today, so nothing visible breaks. The Insight Lab's run and propose paths, and the MCP panel's tool invocation, are among them. Either give each its own page file (for example `pages/api/ml/run.tk` exporting `post`), or delete the ones nothing will call.<br><br>**2026-09-27.** `pages/api/ml/propose.tk` and `pages/api/ml/run.tk` route `postpropose` and `postrun`; regenerating the registry also picked up `connections`, `presentation` and `setup`, which the hand-kept copy lacked. Routing the other seven the same way took `_handlers.tk` to 35 imports, past toke's cap of 32, and the build failed (T-56). They stay unrouted until the cap is raised or the registry is split.<br><br>**Done 2026-09-27.** **The cap:** toke's import limit is a setting, `max_imports` in `tkc.toml` (or `--max-imports`), measured working at the pin in `docs/upstream/repro-2026-09-27/T-56/`. `tkc.toml` sets `max_imports = 40` with a comment (T-56, ooke O-2); the registry now has 35 imports. Compiling the same `_handlers.tk` with that line removed fails with E9010 on its 33rd import. Neither the 64-struct limit (T-54) nor `max_funcs` (T-25) was reached: moke compiles 304 of 304 modules and links. **The routes:** seven page files in ooke's one-get-one-post convention, as `pages/api/ml/{propose,run}.tk` were: `pages/api/mcp/{tools,invoke,broker,memory}.tk` (GET /api/mcp/tools, POST /api/mcp/invoke, GET /api/mcp/broker, GET and POST /api/mcp/memory) and `pages/api/agents/{scan,schema,diary}.tk` (POST /api/agents/scan, POST /api/agents/schema, GET /api/agents/diary). The registry was regenerated with `LOKE_GEN_MOKE_HANDLERS=1`. **What routing exposed, fixed because the answer was otherwise wrong:** (1) the diary read `agent_id` with `http.reqparam`, which reads the route's path parameters and never the query string, so every request answered 400 "agent_id query param is required"; it now reads the query from `http.reqpath`. (2) The schema comparison read each CSV with `json.str`, which turns `\n` into the letter n (T-47), so every file was one line and every diff listed invented columns (`bn1`, `2n`); it uses `jx.strvalue`. (3) `memory.store`, `memory.status` and `memory.context` killed the worker serving the request (the connection closed with no response); `moke.mcp.memorydemo` now refuses those three with an MCP error result naming MK6.6, rather than calling `core.memory.mcpserver`. (4) `templates/mcp.tkt` and `templates/agents.tkt` fetched `/api/moke/mcp/...` and `/api/moke/agents...`, which moke has never served; they fetch the real routes. **Evidence:** `scripts/smoke_serve_moke.sh` gains twelve checks over real HTTP, each judging the body: the tool list names `anonymise`; invoke requires a tool name and reports an unknown one; the broker lists `loke-memory`; the memory panel lists its tools, `memory.diary_write` succeeds and `memory.status` is refused with its reason; a scan of a column with a planted outlier reports an IQR finding on that column; the schema check requires both files and reports "2 changes: 1 added, 1 removed"; the diary answers for `schema-change-detector` and 404s an unknown agent. **Mutants:** removing the seven registrations from `_handlers.tk` failed all twelve (an unrouted GET answers 404; an unrouted POST answers 200 with its own request body echoed back by ooke's static fallback, which only a body check catches). Reverting fixes (1)-(3) failed the diary, schema and `memory.status` checks (the last with no response at all). Every file was restored and checked with `cmp`. **Not done:** the panels' state is per worker process, so a recorded run or invocation is seen by about one request in four (MK6.6); `core.memory.mcpserver` itself is not fixed (MK6.6); nothing asserts what mcp-toke's tools compute (MK6.6). |
| MK6.6 | M | **Done** — 2026-10-07 | **What the newly routed MCP and agents panels still get wrong** — Found 2026-09-27 by MK6.5, which gave these handlers routes and probed them over HTTP. (1) **State is per worker.** `pages/api/mcp.tk` and `pages/api/agents.tk` keep the tool log, the memory log and the agents' run history in module-level `let` state, and moke serves from several pre-forked worker processes (`serverworkers:4` in the generated main, `http_serve_workers` in std.http), so each worker has its own copy: after six invocations, eight reads of `/api/mcp/tools` reported 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1 invocations, and a scan's run did not appear in `/api/agents`. Persist it (the database, or a file), or say it is per session. (2) **`core.memory.mcpserver` kills its caller** on `memory.store`, `memory.status` and `memory.context`: through `/api/mcp/memory` the connection closed with no response and the worker died. It reads `json.dec` results and `palace.status` through `i64` handles (`handlestatusok(s:i64)` reads `s.totaldrawers`) and matches user-sum results (T-18). In the same state memory.diary_write answered `{"ok":true}` for a drawer it never wrote. Fixing those exposed two more: nothing on any write path indexed a drawer (`search.indexdrawer` was never called and could not have worked), so memory.search and memory.facts could never find a stored memory; and once they could, memory.facts and memory.context crashed on `aaak.defaultlevel`'s bare `$medium(0)` (T-13 again). Also: memory.store reported a second random id unrelated to the drawer it wrote, and memory.context's answer was not JSON (raw newlines). **Fix:** `palace.openok` (bool) gates every tool; `palace.statusjson` formats the counts where they are counted and replaces `status`; `storage.writedrawer` (bool) is the write, `storedrawer` keeps its signature over it, and `storage.turndrawer` builds a turn's drawer; `search.indexkeywords` replaces `indexdrawer` and is called inside the drawer's transaction; `aaak.defaultlevel` constructs its variant; `core.memory.mcpserver` reads every argument through a `$ok`-first match, reports the drawer id it wrote, `json.enc`s the context and refuses a store or diary entry with no content. `moke.mcp.memorydemo` no longer refuses the three tools and creates its data directory before each call. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/memory/test_mcp_server.tk` (19 assertions) through `handlememorytool`: status, context and diary_write against a directory that cannot open answer error results; then store, search (finds the note by the id store reported), facts, status (exact counts), context (valid JSON, names the wing and hall), diary_write, and a refused store that writes nothing. Run against the pre-MK6.6 memory modules it crashed with SIGSEGV at its first call. Mutants, each restored and checked with `cmp`: the bare `$public` restored (SIGSEGV); indexing removed (3 assertions fail); the bare `$medium(0)` restored (SIGSEGV); the `openok` gate bypassed ("it says the palace did not open" fails, then SIGSEGV). `smoke_serve_moke.sh` now invokes store, status, search and context through POST /api/mcp/memory and judges each body (store names its drawer, status counts `"total_drawers":2,"total_closets":0,"total_wings":2`, search returns the note, context carries the palace map). **(1) State shared across workers.** moke has no database, and std.db's one connection belongs to the memory palace, so `moke.panellog` (new, `src/panel_log.tk`) keeps each history as a file under `$HOME/.loke/moke`, one line per event, appended with O_APPEND and read back whole. The MCP tool and memory panels append a record and read their history and `total_invocations` from it; the agents' runs are appended as tab-separated lines (index, ids, times, finding count, summary) and the agents are rebuilt from them with the same `status.recordrun` on every read, so the diary sees them too. **The records carry no content:** the history now outlives the request, and a tool such as `anonymise` is handed exactly the text a user wants kept private, so `historyjson` keeps tool, time, duration and success and drops arguments, results and errors; the POST still returns the whole invocation, and `templates/mcp.tkt` shows the result of the call it just made from that answer. **Evidence:** `smoke_serve_moke.sh` makes six tool invocations and five memory calls, then reads eight times each: every read of /api/mcp/tools must report `"total_invocations":6}` and of /api/mcp/memory `5}`, every read of the scanner's diary `"total_runs":1,` and of /api/agents the schema run's summary; and the memory log must hold `"args_json":""` for memory.store. Mutant: the pre-MK6.6 `pages/api/mcp.tk` failed all sixteen MCP reads (each answered from one worker's copy) and the content check; the pre-MK6.6 `pages/api/agents.tk` failed 12 of the first 15 agent reads (the scanner's diary saw its run on reads 1, 4 and 7 only). Both restored and checked with `cmp`. **(4)** `pages/api/upload.tk` reads `?name=` from `http.reqpath` with the diary's `queryvalue`; routing it also showed every preview cell going out as a bare integer, the cell's ADDRESS (`"preview_rows":[[43465735...`), because the row was bound untyped; it is typed. The memory modules' other matches on user-sum results (`search.search` in the MCP server and in context's L2 and L3, `palace.walk` in context's L1, `storeturn`, mining's `storedrawer`) still have `$err` arms that cannot run; with the palace known to be open they are reached only by a failing query, MK6.8. | MK6.7 | S | **Done** — 2026-10-07 | **mcp-toke's `compress` answers `~` for a two-row array, and nothing tests what the mcp-toke tools compute** — Moved from MK6.6 (3), found 2026-09-27 by MK6.5. Through POST /api/mcp/invoke, `compress` answered `{"toon":"~","savings_pct":94}` for `[{"a":1},{"a":2}]`. moke's handler relays the tool's result faithfully, so the fault, if it is one, is in `packages/mcp-toke`. Measure what `compress` returns for small inputs against its specification, and give the tools a test that judges their output. <br><br>**Done 2026-09-28: compress and decompress.** **The cause:** `core.optimiser.toon.jsontotoon` went through `$toonvalue`, whose variants carry only an `i64` tag, so an object or array encoded to `~` whatever it held (the GA1.5 note in `toon.tk` had said so), and `savings_pct` was a real character ratio measured against that tilde: 94. `toontojson` likewise gave back only `[]`, `{}` or `""`. **The fix:** a codec in `toon.tk` that never holds a value in `$toonvalue`: `encodejson` tokenises the JSON text and writes TOON (toon-format/toon) from the tokens; `decodetoon` parses TOON back to JSON; `jsontotoon`/`toontojson` answer their `.text` ("" on failure, as before). It encodes a single value, an object of single values and arrays, an array of single values (`[3]: 1,2,3`), an array of objects sharing one key order (the tabular `[2]{a}:` form) and an empty array; it refuses, naming the reason, a nested object, an array of arrays, mixed arrays, rows whose keys differ, an empty object, an exponent, and the escapes TOON lacks (`\u`, `\/`, `\b`, `\f`). Numbers and escapes are carried as written, so decoding what it encodes gives the input minus insignificant whitespace, byte for byte. mcp-toke's compress reports `json_chars`, `minified_json_chars`, `toon_chars`, `savings_pct` and `savings_vs_minified_pct`, every one measured from `str.len` in the module that took it (the two percentages are integer, truncated, from basis points); for `[{"a":1},{"a":2}]`: `[2]{a}:\n  1\n  2`, 17 and 15 characters, 11%. These are character savings, not token savings (C1 unchanged). A refusal is an MCP error result with the reason and no figures. Also fixed on the way: the arguments were read with `json.getstr` (untyped) and, for decompress, would have lost every `\n` (T-47); they are read with `jx.strvalue`. The TOON was quoted with `json.enc`, which, **measured, escapes a quote but leaves a newline raw**, so every multi-line answer was invalid JSON; it uses `jx.escape` (MK6.11 filed for the same call in the memory MCP server). The unused `format` argument is gone from compress's schema. **Evidence:** `tests/unit/optimiser/test_toon_codec.tk`: 9 exact round trips (the TOON asserted, then decode equals the minified input), 12 refusals with their reasons, 8 malformed documents that must not decode. `tests/unit/mcp_toke/test_compress.tk` (15 assertions) through `handletool`: the TOON and all five figures for the story's input, a padded input (22 characters, 31%; 11% against minified), a negative saving (-42% for `["a,b"]`), a named refusal, decompress back to the original, and a refused bad count. Mutants, each restored and checked with `cmp`: `jsontotoon` put back on the classifier (18 failures in the codec test), nothing quoted (3 in the codec test, 2 in the tool test), the list-count check removed (2 and 1), compress reporting an invented 94 (3 in the tool test). `test_toon.tk`'s assertion that an object encodes to `~` now asserts `name: test\nn: 42`. `smoke_serve_moke.sh` invokes compress through POST /api/mcp/invoke and judges the body for the TOON table and `toon_chars` 15 / `savings_pct` 11 (and, as every check there, that the body is valid JSON); the shared-history reads now count eight invocations. **Not done:** anonymise, profile and analyse are still untested and still read their arguments with `json.getstr` (MK6.10). The codec does not encode nested objects or arrays of arrays; it refuses them. Its decoder reads the TOON it writes, strictly, not all TOON: for example it refuses a bare value that TOON would have quoted.<br><br>**Done 2026-10-07.** What MK6.7 left, anonymise, profile and analyse, went to MK6.10, which is Done (2026-09-28): each now has a test judging its output, and anonymise's answer carries no value it replaced. Nothing of MK6.7's own scope was open, so this pass re-verified it at toke 3.1.0 / ooke 3.0.0-rc.2 (cab2dd7c) and tightened the HTTP evidence for the story's own finding. `smoke_serve_moke.sh`'s two compress checks were substring matches (`[2]{a}:`, and `toon_chars` 15 / `savings_pct` 11), which a TOON with the right header and wrong rows would pass, and decompress had no check through the route. A new `tool_exact` decodes each layer of the POST /api/mcp/invoke answer strictly (Python's `json`) and compares the WHOLE answer: compress of `[{"a":1},{"a":2}]` must equal `{"toon":"[2]{a}:\n  1\n  2","json_chars":17,"minified_json_chars":17,"toon_chars":15,"savings_pct":11,"savings_vs_minified_pct":11}`; decompress of that TOON must equal `{"json":"[{\"a\":1},{\"a\":2}]"}`, the input byte for byte; and compress of `{"a":{"b":1}}` must be a failed call whose error names "nested object" and reports no saving. The shared tool log's reads now count twelve invocations. **Evidence:** smoke passes on the real tree; `tests/unit/mcp_toke` (3 binaries) and `tests/unit/optimiser` (7) pass. Mutants in `packages/mcp-toke/src/tools.tk`, built into moke together (each check judges a different function), then restored from a copy outside the tree and checked with `cmp`: compress quoting `~` instead of the TOON (the check fails: the answer is `{"toon": "~", ...}` with every figure still 15 / 11, which the old `toon_chars` substring check would have passed); decompress answering its TOON argument instead of the decoded JSON (fails: `{"json": "[2]{a}:\n  1\n  2"}`); the refusal's reason dropped (fails: `compress: cannot encode`). Exactly those three of the smoke's checks failed. **Not done:** the codec still refuses, by name, nested objects and arrays of arrays. mcp-toke's own server binary is never linked (`build_trees.sh --no-link=mcptoke_main`), so its tools are tested through `handletool`, `handlerequest` and moke's route, never over mcp-toke's socket (MK6.20). anonymise's caller-chosen detection URLs are MK6.12, an open decision, and unchanged here. |

The MCP server's search and facts handlers branch on `succeeded` and answer an error result. `storage.storeturn` answers the `$drawer` it wrote, or one with an empty id (`storage.isstored`); it has no caller. `mining.minetext` stores through `writedrawer`: it had counted every fact as stored, and now reports "N of M facts could not be stored" in `err`. ## Epic MK7: Demo Readiness

*The three gaps between implemented code and a runnable demo: dataset serving API, unified registry, and static assets.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|

# Epic T: Test Suite

*Comprehensive behavioural test coverage for every module. Tests verify runtime correctness — not just that files compile, but that functions return expected values for known inputs. Each story produces one or more `.tk` test files under `tests/unit/`, `tests/integration/`, or `tests/e2e/`. Every test file exposes a `run_all():bool` entry point that logs `PASS`/`FAIL` per assertion and returns `true` only if every assertion passes.*

*Transform demo datasets from minimal samples into rich, realistic data with deliberate patterns for demonstrating every moke capability. Each dataset should have clear outliers, clusters, time series trends, PII examples, and cross-dataset relationships. Add complementary IT operations datasets for a complete observability scenario.*

Add columns: `os_patch_level`, `last_reboot_days`, `cpu_util_avg`, `ram_util_avg`, `disk_util_avg`, `network_throughput_mbps`, `open_incidents`, `maintenance_window`, `environment` (prod/staging/dev/dr), `criticality` (P1-P4), `application_owner`, `cost_centre`.
