# TOOLCHAIN

## Epic F10: Toolchain Currency and Upstream Feedback

*Get loke building on a current toke and ooke, and keep it there, so it cannot drift four months behind again.*

loke's last commit before this work was 2026-05-21. toke was being committed daily and ooke had moved a
major version past loke's declared `ooke >= 1.0.0` without anyone noticing, because nothing checked.

### The hold criterion, and why it is a commit and not a version

**loke needs toke at commit `6cc9061` or later — in practice a build of `main` — and ooke `v3.0.0-rc.1`.**
`TOOLCHAIN.lock` is the authority; this section explains it.

Upstream is explicit that **no tagged toke release works** and that there is no version number to give.
That is not a preference: toke's `VERSION` file still reads 2.8.0 well past the `v2.8.0` tag, so a semver
comparison would happily accept a checkout that cannot build loke. toke is therefore gated on **commit
ancestry** with its version recorded as advisory only. ooke is gated on a **tag**, which it now has.

**Current position, 2026-09-20: the hold is CLEARED.** Both pins are published and fetchable, which was
itself a blocker — neither was on a remote until now, so CI could not obtain a compiler at any migration
status and no figure this project published was reproducible by anyone else. CI now builds loke and
reproduces the local census exactly.

Accepting a release candidate reverses the earlier decision to wait for a final 3.0.0. That reversal was
deliberate and instructed. What does **not** move is the publication bar: a figure measured against an rc
is labelled with the rc, so if the final tag changes, every affected number can be found again.

**The build is green.** 218 of 218 modules compile, 0 errors, and `packages/browser/build/loke` links (`4d6e0ec` onward). The figures this preamble used to carry — "58 of 199 modules, 52 of 179 interfaces, 291 errors of which 226 were E2030 cascade" — were the 2026-09-20 measurement and are kept here only so they are not mistaken for current. Progress was measured in modules compiling and interfaces emitted rather than in error count, which was dominated by cascade and fell in jumps; that was the right instrument and it is why the intermediate F10.14–F10.19 markers quote ladders that do not join up. **The open work is no longer about making the build compile.** It is F10.23 (the 247 files in six trees the build has never touched), F10.17, F10.21, F10.22 and the wiring stories in GA1.
**226 are `E2030` cascade** from modules that have not compiled yet — so the real work is 65 errors in 19
files, split into F10.14–F10.24 below. Three defects in the build itself were masking this and are fixed:
the interface directory held a stale nested tree toke never read, the interface pass omitted
`--emit-llvm` so every library failed on "no main function", and interfaces were emitted alphabetically
rather than in dependency order.

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| F10.1 | M | **Done** | **Make the build fail loudly** — every compiler invocation in `build_loke.sh` ended `2>/dev/null \|\| true` and it linked with `-Wl,-undefined,dynamic_lookup`, so a build in which every module failed still printed "Done" and produced a binary, turning undefined symbols into runtime crashes. Now reports a per-module census to `build/break-report.txt` and refuses to link an incomplete build. **Re-verified 2026-09-24 (RV1.5).** Exercised by accident, which is the best kind of evidence. Built against toke main `444a55c`, 21 modules failed to type-check. The build printed the census, wrote `build/trees/loke/break-report.txt`, named the one unresolved symbol and ended "Refusing to link an incomplete build" with exit 1. It did not link. |
| F10.2 | M | **Done** | **Path portability** — `run_tests.sh` and `build_test.sh` hardcoded an absolute home path with no environment override while CI exported `TOKE_DIR`, so **CI's test job could never have passed** regardless of code correctness, despite a badge in the README. Both now honour `TOKE_DIR` and fail fast when the compiler is absent instead of reporting every test as a compile error. |
| F10.3 | M | **Done** | **Pin and gate the toolchain** — `TOOLCHAIN.lock` plus `scripts/check_toolchain.sh`, gating toke by commit ancestry and ooke by released version, per the criterion above. CI clones the pinned commits rather than chasing upstream HEAD, which previously meant CI could break on somebody else's commit at random with no local reproduction. |
| F10.4 | S | **Done** | **Drift watch** — pinning alone would let loke drift silently again, which is how it fell four months behind. A scheduled job compares the lock against upstream HEAD weekly and warns without turning `main` red. |
| F10.5 | M | **Done** | **Diagnostics-driven fixer** — `scripts/fix_diagnostics.py` applies mechanical fixes by byte offset from toke's own JSON diagnostics, so only spans the compiler itself flags are touched. This replaces the regex approach in the previous migration script, whose `^[ \t]*//.*\n` silently deleted the licence header from 520 files. 968 equality fixes applied; `packages/` type-check went 167 to 246 passing. **Re-verified 2026-09-24 (RV1.5).** `scripts/fix_diagnostics.py` exists and patches by byte offset from toke's JSON diagnostics, as stated. The "167 to 246 passing" figure is **historical** (2026-09-19, a different compiler and a different tree) and cannot be re-measured. It must not be quoted as a current figure. It is superseded by the 224-module, 0-error build. |
| F10.6 | S | **Done** | **Remove the destructive migration scripts** — their job is finished and a repo-wide destructive rewriter is a standing hazard whether or not its regex is fixed. |
| F10.7 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-22 | **The 209 ceiling was wrong and is withdrawn.** I reported that eight modules were unreachable because `std.tls` / `std.mdns` / `std.infer` / `std.mlx` declare identifiers containing underscores that toke rejects. They are not unreachable: the compiler carries those functions in its builtin table and resolves them regardless of the `.tki`. Their signatures had drifted, that is all, and all eight now compile. What is true instead is worse for the features and better for the build — **all four of those stdlib modules are stubs** that ignore their arguments and return `0` or a sentinel string (`"[infer: not available]"`, `"[mlx: not available]"`). See T-11 in [`docs/upstream/toke-issues.md`](upstream/toke-issues.md). The affected loke modules now report unavailability instead of treating a stub's return as a result — which mattered: `models/infer.tk` fed `privacy/ner_local.tk`, and a sentinel string reaching a PII detector reads as "no entities found".<br><br>Getting from compiling to **linking** was a second phase and larger than the first. Every module compiled while clang rejected the linked IR, with errors that name an LLVM label and no toke source file. Seven toke defects were isolated with minimal reproductions and are filed as T-1 to T-7; four sweeps in `scripts/` now find each class in source or IR, and all five are gate steps. The largest was **T-6: any `let` that shadows an enclosing `let` emits invalid IR** — which is also how a broken accumulator looks, so the same 52 sites were both a link failure and a silent logic bug.<br><br>**Status detail:** **Done** — **217 of 217 modules compile and `packages/browser/build/loke` links.** First green build of this repository. 308 errors → 0 *(Ladder note, settled 2026-09-23: 308 → 0 is the END STATE after every one of F10.14–F10.24 landed, not a rung in the same ladder as their individual steps. It is a summary figure and should not be read as a single story's delta.)* |
| F10.8 | M |  | **Adopt ooke 3.x interfaces** — every shared interface but two had already drifted at 2.0.0 (`store` 40 changes, `template` 33, `router` 15), plus two new modules. A major version means more. Note `packages/browser/_serve_main.tk` is generated by a heredoc inside `build_loke.sh`, so the build script changes, not just source.<br><br>**Partly covered by F10.39 (2026-10-01):** the move to ooke 3.0.0-rc.2 adopted the rc.2 `$ookecfg` (sixteen fields, `serverhost` new) and `serve.serverun`'s host parameter in both generated server mains, and compiles rc.2's generated `ooke.floor` and a placeholder `ooke.handlers` into `build/ooke-objs`. Adopting the drifted `store`, `template` and `router` interfaces in loke's own code is not done there and stays here. |
| F10.9 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-28 | **Capability manifest** — toke has a capability broker with runtime traps for ungranted capabilities, and loke declares nothing. Add a `tkc.toml` with a **minimal, justified** grant set and document why each is granted. This is also an opportunity rather than a chore: a minimal audited grant set is a real, verifiable privacy property to replace some unverified claims.<br><br>**Done 2026-09-28.** **How the binaries ran before:** toke at the pin (`0b0bc4e`) is deny-by-default. A probe making one gated call per class (`file.read`, `file.write`, `net.portavailable`, `process.spawn`, `env.set`), built with an empty manifest, traps `CAP001` on all five, and each passes with its `--allow-*` flag. loke did declare grants: `tkc.toml` has had a `[capabilities]` table since 2026-09-22 (NC1.9), and `scripts/lib/build_tree.sh` and `scripts/run_tests.sh` pass it with `--config=` to every compile. The grants are baked into the module that defines `main` (`@__tk_cap_baked_grants`). No script in the repository passes an `--allow-*` flag at run time. So loke, moke, loke-cli and every test binary ran with what that table granted, which was **all five classes (0x1f)**. Its `env = true` line was commented "provider API keys come from the environment", but reading the environment is not gated, and `env` is toke's short spelling of `env_write`. The line granted environment WRITE, the one class nothing uses, while a comment lower down said env.write was not granted. Its quoted scopes (`read = "~/.loke"`, `net = "127.0.0.1"`) were ignored. **What changed:** `tkc.toml` now grants `fs_read`, `fs_write`, `net` and `process_spawn` as bare `true`, 0x17, and sets `env_write = false`. Nothing in loke, moke, loke-cli or ooke calls `env.set` or `os.setenv`. Each grant carries the files, ports or executables it serves, what breaks without it (measured), and its intended scope. **Scoping:** the broker cannot scope. A binary built with `fs_read = "/nonexistent-dir-only"` read `/etc/hosts`, and one built with `net = "10.255.255.1:9"` bound a loopback port. The grants are therefore written as `true`, so no line reads as a limit that does not exist. Loopback-only network is NOT a property of the manifest. It rests on `core.providers.transport` refusing non-loopback sends (T-58 hold), and the servers still bind every interface (T-43). Filed as **T-59** in `docs/upstream/toke-issues.md`, which also records that a launcher can add any class with `--allow-*` at any argv position, and that `enforce = false` does not opt out, contrary to toke's docs. **Evidence:** `scripts/check_capabilities.sh`, new and in the gate's Build step, builds `scripts/lib/cap_probe.tk` with the repository's `tkc.toml`. It asserts that the manifest parses to 0x17, that the four granted classes return, that `env_write` aborts with `CAP001: capability 'env.write'`, and that all three built entry modules bake 23. Mutants: restoring `env = true` failed 2 checks (grants 0x1f; the probe's `env.set` succeeded), and `process_spawn = false` failed 2. `tkc.toml` was restored and checked with `cmp`. **Per-class mutants on the real binaries:** each binary's entry module was recompiled with one grant removed and relinked against the production objects (only that module carries the grants). The mutant was then run through the binary's own smoke under the e2e lock, and the production binary was restored and checked with `cmp`. Without `process_spawn`, loke's /api/health, /api/models, /api/pipeline, /installer and /sysmon drop the connection, and so do moke's /api/health, /api/pipeline and /api/ml/propose. loke-cli's doctor fails "says Ollama is not running", because it confirms a down service with `nc`. `smoke_benchmark` does not spawn and passes. A denied call exits the whole process, so in a server it shows as a dropped connection, not an error response. **Not done:** per-path, per-host and per-executable scoping, and a way to forbid run-time `--allow-*` escalation, both wait on upstream (T-59). The runtime's own bad handle is NULL: with `$err:e 0`, measured, `process.stdout` takes its `$err` arm, `process.wait` answers -1, `process.kill` false and `h==0` is true, so even a missed check fails closed. **Fixed** (error arm now `0`, tested with `h==0` before any read or wait, each site reporting failure the way it already meant to): `cli.updater.runcmd` and `cli.sign.runcmd` (127, "could not spawn command" — the check was also inverted, `if(!(h == @())){}el{...}`), `cli.portable.chmod755` (false), `shared.reachability.connects` and `localdelete` (false), `core.monitoring.sysmon` (five spawns, plus `getactivemodel`, whose error arm was `""`), and `core.installer.install`'s Windows installer, Linux install script and `verifyinstallat` spawns, whose error arm was the `$installresult` struct itself, so a failed spawn waited on the struct's address. Test harness spawns in 33 test files (`tests/` and `packages/moke/tests/test_proxy_fetch.tk`) changed the same way. **Gate:** `scripts/find_empty_array_sentinel.py` in quality-gate.sh's static checks, over `packages tests scripts` (skipping `build`, `_archived-tests`, `.claude`): flags any `== @()`/`!= @()` outside comments, and any `process.spawn` match that passes the handle through with an `$err` arm other than `0` (direct, or through a name bound to `process.spawn(`). On the pre-fix tree it failed with 202 sites; now OK. Known exception, capped at its current 4 hits so a new one still fails: `packages/moke/src/proxy/fetch.tk` (`runout`, `fetchpinned`), owned by the MK19.9 review fix (finding 1, W54). The other excluded areas (`packages/browser/pages/api/pipeline.tk`, `packages/core/src/privacy/pipeline.tk`, `packages/core/src/router/`) contain no instance. **Evidence.** `tests/unit/cli/test_spawn_failure.tk` re-execs itself under a perl alarm (so a hang is a kill, not a hung gate): `--abs` drives `cli.updater.runcmd` on `/nonexistent/f10-44/no-such-tool` (127, the message, no output; a real command still runs); `--nopath` runs with `PATH=/nonexistent/f10-44` and drives `portable.chmod755`, `reachability.connects`, `sysmon.getramstats`/`getcpustats`. On the pre-fix tree: the `--abs` child failed both runcmd assertions, and under the parent the `--nopath` child failed `chmod755` with its output lost (undefined behaviour on the bogus handle). **Mutant:** the idiom put back in `updater.runcmd` — the test failed (`updater.runcmd: a command that cannot start reports 127`, and the message) and the gate check failed on updater.tk:76 and :80; restored, cmp identical. **Not done:** ~~`packages/moke/src/proxy/fetch.tk` (W54/MK19.9 review)~~ the proxy's two sites are done (2026-10-01, MK19.9 review finding 1): `runspawn` and `fetchwith` use the handle only inside the match's `$ok` arm and refuse from the `$err` arm, killed by a spawnchild case in `test_proxy_fetch.tk`; the known exception is removed from `find_empty_array_sentinel.py`. The `--nopath` assertions passed on the pre-fix tree when run directly, so only the updater path is a stable mutant-killer; the others are no-hang and fail-closed checks. `cli.sign.runcmd` and the installer spawns are fixed but not driven by a test (sign shares the `$cmdresult` name with updater; the installer's spawns need a fake platform). `src/` (legacy, not built) was not swept. |

# DEMO LAYER — moke: DATASETS AND PERSONAL USE

> **Scope note.** Everything in this section is **moke**, the demo application, not loke core. Demo
> datasets, guided flows, import paths and the personal-finance workspace all live in
> `packages/moke/`. loke core gains nothing dataset-specific from these epics — where a story needs a
> core capability it depends on an NC1, DA1 or AD1 story rather than adding domain logic to core.
> The test corpora under `tests/fixtures/` are the exception and are deliberately core: they test the
> detector, not the demo.

## Epic MK19: Government Open Data Expansion

*Broaden the demo beyond synthetic data with real, attributed, offline-first snapshots of Australian government open data, each arriving complete with its own prompts, dashboard and flow.*

The current 15 datasets are synthetic despite being labelled "Government Open Data", and the enrichment
recorded in MK8 landed only in the frontend, so the backend still holds pre-enrichment row counts. Three
different wrong dataset counts appear across the docs. This epic replaces guesswork with attributed
snapshots and one manifest that drives everything.

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| MK19.1 | M | **Done** — 2026-10-01 | **Decide the canonical store and stop the split** — Two divergent dataset stores exist: `packages/moke/data/*.tk` with `data/registry.tk`, served by `pages/api/datasets.tk`, and a `var DATASETS` object inline in `templates/index.tkt` which is **230KB of data and UI fused together**. `grep "api/moke/datasets"` returns zero hits, so the backend path is orphaned and the frontend object is what the demo uses. The two hold different dataset sets. Pick one — recommended: a static manifest plus CSV snapshots under `static/data/`, fetched lazily, because it needs no recompilation, is diffable and reviewable, and drops the weight of `/` from 230KB to about 25KB. Also fix `registry.tk::listall()`, which has an `if` where a loop belongs and therefore returns only one AU dataset.<br><br>**Done 2026-10-01.** Picked the store the row recommended: `packages/moke/static/data` — `manifest.json` names each dataset and points at one CSV under `fixtures/` (synthetic) or `snapshots/` (real). It is now the ONLY store, and every reader uses it. MK19.9 therefore fetches with the system curl (`--resolve`, `--max-filesize`, `--max-time`). Ask upstream for: a resolver returning every address; a client option to connect to a given address while verifying the certificate against the name (curl's --resolve); a body-size limit enforced while reading; a whole-request deadline. ## Epic MK21: Personal Finance Workspace

*The demo where the no-custody claim is tested to destruction: import your own bank statements, structure and analyse them entirely on-device, and use the model to build the analysis without ever showing it the data.*

**Why this epic matters more than the others.** Every other dataset in moke is public or synthetic, so
"no data left the device" is a claim nobody has to trust. A bank statement is the opposite: it is
genuinely the user's, it is maximally sensitive, and nobody would accept "we redact it first" as an
answer — which is precisely the argument the external literature supports
(`docs/research/disclosure-measurement-findings.md` §1). If any personal financial value leaves the
device during a session in this workspace, the architecture claim in NC1 has failed. This workspace is
therefore both the flagship demonstration and the hardest test.

**What the model is for, and what it is never given.** The model helps *build the analysis* — proposing
a category taxonomy, generating the query or rule set, explaining what a tax category generally covers.
It is never given a transaction, a merchant, an amount, an account number or a balance. Merchant names
in particular are not "low sensitivity": a pharmacy, a clinic, a solicitor or a gambling site each
discloses something material about a person, so merchant text is treated as personal data throughout and
never leaves, not even for categorisation.

> **Two things this epic must say plainly to the user, not bury.**
>
> 1. **Storage is not encrypted today.** The database encryption pragma is inert (X8), so imported
>    statements would sit in plaintext on disk. Personal financial data makes that materially worse than
>    it is for demo data. Either X8 lands first, or this workspace keeps its data in a separately
>    encrypted store, or it refuses to persist at all and works per-session. **MK21.2 decides this, and
>    it gates the rest of the epic.**
> 2. **This is not tax advice, and it does not lodge anything.** It organises figures and shows its
>    working so a person or their accountant can check it. Any output that looks like a determination
>    must be labelled as an estimate with its method shown.

Not fixable in loke except by making the datasets smaller or loading them from files rather than literals — **and loading them from files is probably right anyway**, since a demo dataset compiled into the binary cannot be changed without a rebuild. **(b) T-37 — a declared `@f64` gets the SCALAR f64 conversion applied to its array handle — 4 modules, plus one of a different kind.** Reduced to a three-line reproduction: `f=retf64arr(a:@f64;v:f64):@f64{ <a.push(v) }` emits `fptosi double %t4 to i64` on the array HANDLE and clang refuses it, while the identical `@str` and `@i64` forms emit `ptrtoint` and are correct. It is not only the return position — a struct field declared `@f64` does the same, so wrapping the array is not a workaround, and routing every assignment through a helper only moves the error into the helper (measured, then reverted). `@(@f64)` IS correct, which is why it looks intermittent: in `ml/engine.tk` the k-means matrix is fine while every single-vector helper (`zerovector`, `centroidfor`, `extractnumericcol`) is not. Affected `moke_compute` (`%datesums`), `moke_hooks` (`%nums`), `moke_profiler` (`%nums`) and `moke_ml_engine` (`%point`). **`profiler` and `hooks` are FIXED**: their accumulators are now `@i64` of micro-units (1e6, so the four decimal places they print survive exactly) reading through the new `shared.types.f64micro`/`micro2f64`/`i64min`/`i64max`/`i64mean`. Both assembled immediately. That is a real fix and not only a workaround — integer summation is more accurate for a mean than accumulating over f64 — but it is cheap only where the consumers are simple statistics. **`compute` and `ml_engine` remain**, and for a stated reason: `compute` uses `math.percentile` and `math.linreg` over `@f64`, and `ml_engine` is a k-means implementation; neither has an integer equivalent in `std.math`, so both need the arithmetic reimplemented rather than retyped. A fifth workaround was measured and also fails — wrapping the column in a one-row `@(@f64)`, which is the container shape T-37 handles correctly, does not help because the INNER accumulator is still an `@f64` local. **There is no loke-side fix that keeps an f64 vector**: the options are a fixed-point `@i64` — hundredths or basis points, as T-20 already forces elsewhere — or `@(@f64)` indexed as a single row, and either changes the type of every producer and consumer. For k-means that means rewriting the arithmetic, so it is filed rather than forced. `core.optimiser.cache.tof64` returns `@f64` and is SAFE, because its accumulator is only ever self-updated and so takes the in-place path — that is the discriminator for anyone fixing it. **`moke_costcomparison` was the fifth and is FIXED**: `'%t93' defined with type 'double' but expected 'i32'`, where `let incost=(tokensin / 1000) * costin` divided an `i32` by 1000 as an INTEGER — so every request under 1,000 tokens was costed at zero and every other rounded down to a whole thousand. Now `((tokensin as f64) / 1000.0) * costin` with both locals annotated `:f64`. **Done 2026-09-24: moke links, serves, and loads every dataset.** (a) T-35: the 17 demo datasets moved from source literals to `packages/moke/data/csv/*.csv`. The extraction was mechanical and checked each row was as wide as its header. They load through the new `moke.data.loader`, which reuses `moke.upload.parsecsv`. A dataset that cannot be read comes back empty and is logged, not partial. (b) T-37: `compute.optimeseries` accumulates integer micro-units, formatted with integer arithmetic only, so no f64 crosses a module (T-20). `compute.opcorrelate` and `ml.engine.featurematrix` build each `@f64` in a helper function (`pairedside`, `pointof`), the shape that assembles. **Result:** 279 of 279 modules compile, every object assembles, 0 unresolved symbols, and a 2.1 MB `build/trees/moke/moke`. **Evidence, against the running server:** `scripts/smoke_serve_moke.sh` requests 11 pages and POSTs every registry id to `/api/datasets`. All 17 load with exactly the column and row counts the literals had. That was checked id by id when first served (for example au.medicare 26x30, it_platform.wc_orders 12x80). Running it for the first time found `/` and `/chat` returning 500 "Handler returned null" (LS1.1u). moke is now built by `quality-gate.sh --step build`, and its smoke test runs in the test step. |
| MK21.17 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-24 | **`std.csv` exists now, and moke's hand-rolled parser has one real gap** — unblocked by toke's Epic 135: `std.csv` is at the pinned `0b0bc4e` with 18 functions, including `csv.sniff(@(byte)) -> csvdialect!csverr` (dialect detection, which `upload.detectdelimiter` approximates by counting occurrences), `csv.reader`/`csv.next`/`csv.header`, `csv.parse`, `csv.raggedreport(csvreader) -> @(str)` for malformed rows, and `csv.lasterrline() -> u64`. **First, the good news, because it decides the priority:** `upload.splitcsvline` is CORRECT for quoted fields — it tracks `inquotes` and handles the doubled-quote escape — so this is not a correctness emergency and the parser should not be replaced casually. **The gap is a newline INSIDE a quoted field.** `upload.parsecsv` calls `datalines` first, which splits the whole text on newlines before any quote state exists, so a field like `"123 Smith St\nSydney"` becomes two rows — and every subsequent column in the file shifts by one. For this epic that is worse than a parse error: values land in the wrong columns, so the column the sensitivity classifier reads is not the column the value came from, and a PII field can be classified as PUBLIC because its header says something harmless. A multi-line address is ordinary data in exactly the kind of spreadsheet this demo loads. **Scope:** replace `parsecsv`'s internals with a `csv.reader` loop, keep `guessname`/`validate`/`gencolheaders`, and keep `padfields` only if `csv.raggedreport` does not cover it. Note `csv.reader` takes `[byte]` and a `u8` delimiter, so the plumbing differs from `str`-based splitting. Assert the multi-line-quoted-field case first, red, before touching the parser — that is the only assertion that distinguishes the new code from the old. # AUDIT-DRIVEN GAPS

> **Generated:** 2026-05-20 — Full audit of specification, design principles, and architecture against actual implementation. These epics address gaps where the vision has not aligned with what was built.

## Epic GA1: Pipeline Integration — Wire Core Engine into Browser

*Written when the browser API handler bypassed the core engine entirely. **Five of the nine wirings now exist at HEAD** — privacy pipeline, response restoration, kill switch, audit logging and policy evaluation. Four do not: the optimiser, the semantic cache, the router (the provider is still chosen by an if/else on API-key length), and therefore the end-to-end verification. Corrected 2026-09-19 against the committed tree; see `docs/claims.md` A13 for the line-level evidence.*

> **Do not read the working tree for this epic's status.** The uncommitted copy of `pipeline.tk` strips all nine core imports and is a regression, not the state of the repository (F10.13, X8.5).

Across midnight those two reads disagree, so the persisted usage is discarded and the day's spend silently resets to zero **mid-request**. Observed: `tests/integration/test_pipeline_api.tk`'s assertion *"a manager built after the write carries the persisted token count"* failed once in a full-suite run that crossed 00:00, and passed on every run before and after — including twice in isolation immediately afterwards. The window is one comparison wide, which is why it reads as flakiness; the consequence is that a user who exceeds a daily budget at 23:59:59 is not blocked at 00:00:00, which is arguably correct, and one who is at their limit mid-request has the limit vanish, which is not. Fix by threading ONE day number through the request — compute it once where the request starts and pass it to both — rather than calling the clock twice. A test that fakes the clock across a boundary is the only way to assert it; `t.esttokens`-style injection of a timestamp parameter is the cheap route. **Closed 2026-09-24.** The consequence stated above was wrong in its direction, corrected here: in `completed()` the manager was built with one clock read and persisted with a second, so across 00:00 the load saw day N-1, loaded yesterday's usage, added the request and stamped the sum with day N. ## Epic GA2: Security Hardening

*API keys stored in plaintext JSON, SQLite unencrypted, no license headers. These are specification requirements that are not met.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| GA2.1 | L | **Reopened** — keys already in settings.json are never migrated, and were the only keys read | **Migrate API keys to OS keychain** — Replace `~/.loke/settings.json` plaintext key storage with OS keychain integration. On macOS use Security framework via toke/ooke bindings. Keys fetched per-request with expiry validation, never written to disk, never appear in logs. Update `settings.tk` handler and all consumers. Spec: "Secrets and API keys stored in OS keychain, NEVER in config files." **Reopened 2026-09-24 (RV1.4).** "Never written to disk" is false in practice. Saving a key through `/api/settings` moves it to the keychain and removes it from `settings.json`, and that part works. **Nothing migrates a key that is already in `settings.json`.** Measured on the development machine: both provider keys were still there in plaintext (only their presence and length were read, not their values). Until X4.7 the request path read ONLY `settings.json`, so the keychain was never consulted for a request. "Fetched per-request with expiry validation" has no implementation. Remaining work: a one-time migration on first read, which moves the key to the keychain and removes it from the file, with a test using a temporary settings path. Also a decision on expiry validation, which no provider key actually carries. Claim A9 is corrected to `partial`. |
| GA2.2 | M | **Reopened** | **Enable SQLCipher encryption** — Switch from plaintext SQLite to SQLCipher for `~/.loke/loke.db`. Derive encryption key from OS keychain. All tables encrypted at rest. Spec: "All tables encrypted at rest via SQLCipher from OS keychain secret."<br><br>**Status detail:** **Reopened — see X8.1.** Not done: `PRAGMA key` is issued and silently ignored by plain SQLite, so the database is plaintext on disk. SQLCipher is not available in the toolchain and may never be; the replacement approach is field-level `std.encrypt` under X8.2 |

# NO-CUSTODY ARCHITECTURE

> **Why this layer exists**
>
> loke's original core path is: detect PII, substitute placeholders, send the redacted text to an
> external model. Peer-reviewed work establishes that this is not an effective privacy defence —
> large models infer and re-identify obscured entities from surrounding context (Staab et al.,
> ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.07298; Staab et al., ICLR 2025, arXiv:2402.13846; RUPTA, arXiv:2407.11770;
> the Text Anonymization Benchmark, *Computational Linguistics* 48(4), 2022). Redaction reduces
> disclosure; it does not prevent identification.
>
> The architecture that does not depend on redaction working is one where **the model never receives
> the data at all**: loke sends a schema profile and the user's intent, the model returns an
> executable artifact, and loke runs that artifact locally against data that never leaves the device.
>
> **Before writing or repositioning any claim in this layer, read
> `docs/research/disclosure-measurement-findings.md`.** It records what the external literature
> already establishes, what remains genuinely open, and — in §8 — a list of nine things loke must not
> claim because they are already published or are definitions rather than findings.
>
> loke already implements this, in one place, without having named it. moke's Insight Lab sends only
> column names, receives an analysis specification, and executes it locally
> (`packages/moke/src/ml/proposal.tk`, `packages/moke/templates/insight.tkt`). This layer makes that
> pattern the primary architecture rather than an accident, and demotes anonymise-and-send to an
> explicitly-labelled fallback for the cases that genuinely require prose in the prompt.

## Epic NC1: No-Custody Artifact Execution

*Make schema-out / artifact-back / execute-locally the default path. The model receives names, types and intent; it never receives rows.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| NC1.1 | M | **Done** | **Define the artifact contract** — Specify the closed operation set an artifact may express, building on the existing `$dashboard` DDL (`packages/moke/src/ddl.tk`) and the 15 operations in `packages/moke/src/compute.tk` (`opcount`, `opsum`, `opavg`, `opmin`, `opmax`, `opgroup`, `optimeseries`, `optopn`, `opdistribution`, `opcorrelate`, `oppercentile`, `opcountby`, `oplatest`, `opdistinct`, `opjoin`). The set MUST remain non-Turing-complete and MUST NOT include arbitrary code: toke exposes no sandboxing primitive (`process.tki` offers spawn/wait/kill only, with no jail, resource cap or syscall filter), so a closed op set is the only safe design. Write `docs/specifications/artifact-contract.md` with the grammar, the validation rules, and the explicit rejection criteria. |
| NC1.2 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-27 | **No-custody schema profile** — Build a profile emitter that carries column names, inferred types, cardinality, null-rate and row count, and **nothing else**. A result that would cross it is computed locally and withheld, and a spent session is refused before anything runs. **`SESSION_PREDICATE_REPEAT_LIMIT` = 20** caps filtered runs per filter column per session. (e) Migrations 37 to 39 were the next free versions at `d34b25a`, and a concurrent branch that also takes 37 will need renumbering at merge. |

## Epic EM1: Exposure Metric

*A disclosure measure that is defined, computed and validated — not asserted. Depends on DA1 and research spike RS2.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| EM1.1 | M | **Done** | **Specify the metric on established axes** — Adopt the three axes already established for disclosure risk — **singling out, linkability, inference** — each as a *control-corrected* rate, rather than inventing a scheme (`docs/research/disclosure-measurement-findings.md` §4). A vector, never a weighted-sum scalar with hand-chosen weights. Quasi-identifier *combination* presence is the strongest single component; presence of any real value is a **gate, not a summand**; bytes and tokens are the strawman baseline to beat, not a privacy measure. State the threat model per component — mixing provider-side linkage, third-party analytics exposure and model memorisation into one number is the specific error the consensus literature warns against. If a single display number is needed, present it explicitly as a lossy projection of the validated vector. |
| EM1.2 | L |  | **Validate the metric, do not assert it** — In the order of persuasiveness set out in `docs/research/disclosure-measurement-findings.md` §7: (a) **dose-response** — inject disclosure of known magnitude and show the metric scales with the dose; (b) **Spearman ρ against attack success across ≥30–50 *configurations*** (arm × dataset × model × redaction level, not individual requests) with bootstrap intervals; (c) against **two structurally different attacks** — linkage and attribute inference — since validating only against the attack the metric was built around is circular; (d) reported as **TPR at low FPR on a log ROC**, not AUC, because one confident identification is the breach. Skip membership inference against model weights: prompts to a frontier API are not training data under standard retention, and reaching for it looks like instrument-shopping. If the metric does not correlate, report that. |
| EM1.3 | M |  | **Comparative measurement across arms** — Report exposure for the three arms of CB1 (data-in-prompt, schema-only, full no-custody) on the same workload, so the architectural claim is quantified as *relative reduction*, never as elimination. |
| EM1.4 | S |  | **Surface through the Scorecard pattern** — `docs/design-principles.md:145` already defines an ambient, queryable scorecard tracking "privacy, cost, compliance, local ratio". Exposure belongs there, not in a warning. |
| EM1.5 | S | **Done** | **State the limits** — Publish, alongside the metric, what it cannot measure: inference from context, provider-side retention and training, and correlation across accounts. The metric bounds disclosure, not consequence. |

Worse, measured: "Bob" (0.95) overlapping "Bob Jones" (0.78) discarded the **longer** entity, and the anonymised prompt was `[PERSON_…] Jones signed.` — the surname forwarded to the provider in the clear. A second leak path, independent of the one PL1.1 closed. Replaced by `strictlyshadows` + `shadowedbyany`, evaluated over the **whole** input list: a candidate is dropped only when another entity's span covers it, its value **strictly contains** the candidate's, and it is at least as confident. Value containment is the load-bearing part — dropping an entity means nothing substitutes its value, so it is only safe when a survivor's value contains it, which `applytotext`'s longest-first order then handles. The relation is transitive and antisymmetric, so survivors are the maximal elements and no pair can shadow each other into both being dropped. **Spanless entities are explicitly out of scope and cannot be made order-independent**: the regex layer sets `start:0;end:0` on everything (PL1.7), so every span is identical and empty; requiring a non-empty span on both sides means such an entity neither shadows nor is shadowed, which is byte-for-byte the previous outcome. 41 assertions, 7 of them red against the unmodified pipeline. *Amended 2026-09-23:* PL1.7 has since landed and the regex layer reports real spans, so shadowing is live for it and the spanless carve-out described here now covers the two NER layers only. Over-detection is fail-safe for redaction and **not** for sensitivity — that label drives routing and gating, so a phone number silently promoted a request to the most restricted tier. Fixed by a boundary check rejecting a match with a digit immediately either side, applied to the seven bare-digit-run patterns, **inside the detection loop before the sensitivity maximum is taken** so a rejected match cannot escalate the label. Recorded in `docs/metrics-baseline.md` as a second dated block rather than by overwriting the first, because the 2026-09-19 figures are what earlier claims were made against. Remaining tail: `au_tfn` still fires inside `au_abn`, where the boundary check cannot help because the neighbouring characters are spaces.* |

| PL1.7 | S | **Done** | *Done 2026-09-23.* **The regex layer supplies no spans, so overlap resolution cannot work on it** — Found 2026-09-23 (PL1.1). `regex.rundetection` set `start:0;end:0` on **every** entity it emitted, so `strictlyshadows` compared the same empty span every time and shadowing never fired for the only detection layer that runs without a network sidecar. **This story's own premise was wrong and is corrected here:** toke's regex engine exposes **no match offset anywhere** — `str.findall`, `str.find`, `str.matches`, `str.countre` and `str.replacere` are all typed `(i64,i64)->i64` in the stdlib interface and none returns a position — so "the regex engine has them" was not true. The offsets are recovered from the matched **value** instead: `str.indexof` over the remainder of the text from a cursor that advances past each match, which relies on `str.findall` returning matches left-to-right (measured, on a 19-digit run). A value occurring twice therefore gets two distinct spans rather than the first one twice — measured on `"0412 345 678 and again 0412 345 678"`, now spans 0–12 and 23–35. A value that cannot be located from the cursor keeps the old `0/0` rather than being given an invented offset, because a fabricated span would silently mis-drive dedup. Shadowing is now live for this layer; the spanless carve-out documented in PL1.9 covers the two NER layers only. 41 assertions in `tests/unit/privacy/test_regex_spans.tk`. | PL1.12 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-24 | **The Ollama NER layer detects nothing and reports itself healthy** — Found 2026-09-24 (PL1.11), and **executed, not inferred**: a probe test against the real `core.privacy.ner` got **zero** entities from `parsecontent("[{\"type\":\"PERSON\",\"value\":\"Alice\"}]")` and zero from `parseresponse` on a well-formed Ollama `/api/chat` body. Not covered: a live Ollama round trip, and whether a given model follows the requested format. claims.md A3 stays `partial` for that reason. |

# VERIFICATION PROGRAMME

> **Why this layer exists**
>
> loke publishes specific numbers — token reduction, pipeline overhead, classification latency,
> compression ratio, retrieval latency, cache hit rate — and none of them is produced by a
> measurement. The methodology, however, already exists and is genuinely rigorous:
> `docs/research/toon-benchmark-methodology.md` specifies named baselines, twelve task types, four
> data shapes, a licensed dataset table, N with warm-up discard, BCa bootstrap confidence intervals,
> Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Benjamini-Hochberg correction, Cliff's delta, SHA-256 frozen snapshots
> and judge calibration against human annotation. `docs/research/research-proposal.md` §5.2 specifies
> per-entity precision/recall/F1 and marginal recall per added detection layer.
>
> The task is therefore **implementation, not design**. One thing must be built first: `std.test`
> exposes three assertion functions over string comparison and cannot record a numeric result, so
> today a test can prove a threshold was met but cannot publish the value it measured.

## Epic VM1: Verification Measurement Substrate

*Build the apparatus that lets a measurement be recorded, repeated and reproduced. Prerequisite for every other story in this layer.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| VM1.1 | M | **Done** | **Numeric result sink** — A structured results file (one JSON object per measurement) carrying the value, units, N, the workload identifier, the tokenizer where relevant, the model and its pinned version, the seed, the timestamp and the toolchain commit from `TOOLCHAIN.lock`. `std.test` cannot carry a number, so measurement runs must write results directly rather than asserting through the test harness. |
| VM1.2 | S | **Done** | **Pin what is currently unpinned** — `packages/privacy-filter/server.py:34-38` loads `openai/privacy-filter` with no revision, so the model is whatever the hub resolves at first run. Pin the revision. Record every external model's exact version string in each result. |
| VM1.3 | M | **Done** — 2026-09-28 | **Repetition and intervals** — Run each configuration N times with the first run discarded as warm-up, and report BCa bootstrap confidence intervals, exactly as `docs/research/toon-benchmark-methodology.md` already specifies. No single-run number may be published.<br><br>**Before 2026-09-28:** Partial. Repetition with warm-up discard was in `benchmarks/lib/result.py`, but the interval was a percentile bootstrap, labelled as such, and nothing stopped a single run of a varying quantity from being recorded.<br><br>**Done 2026-09-28.** **BCa.** `result.bca_ci` is the bias-corrected and accelerated interval of the mean (Efron and Tibshirani 14.3: z0 from the share of the bootstrap distribution below the estimate, ties counted half; the acceleration from the jackknife), and `summarise()` now attaches it. Up to seven kept runs the bootstrap distribution is enumerated exactly (all n^n resamples, grouped by multiset and weighted by multinomial count), so it needs no seed; past seven it draws 10 000 seeded resamples. The method label says which. Identical runs make BCa undefined (0/0), so the interval is the point and is labelled `degenerate`. The percentile function is removed. **Reference:** `scipy.stats.bootstrap(method='BCa')` accepts a bootstrap distribution through `bootstrap_result` with `n_resamples=0`, so it was handed exactly the distribution loke built, and the two agree to 1e-12 on four data sets (4, 5 and 7 runs enumerated, 12 sampled). The comparison runs live where scipy is installed and against values frozen from scipy 1.17.1, so it still bites without scipy. The same test shows BCa moving the upper bound of right-skewed timings well past the percentile bound. **Enforced repetition.** `result.validate` now refuses a measurement that varies between runs (anything with a `model`, anything timed by units such as `ms` or `MB/s`, or a latency, throughput or duration metric) unless it records `runs` ≥ 2 and an interval, and refuses a repeated measurement whose interval is not BCa. A figure computed exactly from fixed inputs (token counts, recall over the committed corpus) is recorded once, since repeating it cannot change it. Every figure reaches `docs/metrics-baseline.md` through this sink, so this is where the rule is enforced. **toke side.** New `core.eval.interval.bca` computes the same interval by the same enumeration, over integer millionths so that the comparisons deciding z0 are exact, and returns bounds rounded outward to the millionth (no f64 crosses a module boundary, T-20). `core.eval.resultsink`'s `$measurement` gains `runs`, `cilow`, `cihigh` and `cimethod` (now at toke's 16-field limit, T-53), writes them, and makes the same refusals as `result.validate`. `loke benchmark` gains `--runs <3-8>` (default 5, the methodology's N for local models): it runs the case set that many times, prints each run with the first marked as the discarded warm-up, and records `keyword_score` and `latency_mean` as the mean of the kept runs, with `runs`, `n` = cases × kept runs, and the BCa interval. Fewer than three or more than eight runs are refused before anything is dispatched. **Evidence.** `benchmarks/lib/test_result.py` (11 tests, in the quality gate). Python mutants, each killed: no acceleration (8 failures), no bias correction (7), no repetition rule (1), a percentile interval accepted (1). `tests/unit/eval/test_interval.tk` (22 assertions) holds `core.eval.interval` to `bca_ci`'s values within one millionth for 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7 runs, both skews, the degenerate case and the refusals; with the acceleration zeroed, 6 assertions failed. `tests/unit/eval/test_resultsink.tk` gained 14 assertions on the repetition fields and refusals; with the repetition refusal disabled, 4 failed. `tests/unit/cli/test_commands.tk` gained 10 on `--runs` parsing. `scripts/smoke_benchmark.sh` (in the gate) now runs five runs against the stand-in Ollama, which delays replies by a cycled list so the kept runs time differently. It checks 25 requests, `runs` = 4, the degenerate score interval, that `latency_mean` is the mean of the four kept runs and not the warm-up, and that the interval the toke binary wrote equals `result.bca_ci` over the per-run means the CLI printed. With the toke acceleration zeroed, that smoke check FAILED. The mutants were run again on the final code, after a lint-only inlining. **Not done:** (1) `docs/metrics-baseline.md`'s "How to add a figure" step 3 still allows "a single observation"; that file belongs to another worker today, so the wording is left for the integrator to align with this rule. (2) Nothing mechanically ties a figure in `docs/metrics-baseline.md` to a recorded row, so a hand-typed figure there is caught only by review: VM1.3a. (3) The two regex-throughput tables already published carry percentile intervals in their result rows; they were not re-measured. (4) `loke benchmark` runs its repetitions back to back in one process; the methodology's 30-minute temporal clustering is met trivially, but no cross-process repetition is offered. (5) `core.eval.interval` computes 95 per cent intervals only as used (any confidence is accepted but only 0.95 is tested), and refuses more than seven kept runs rather than sampling. |
| VM1.3a | S | **Done** — 2026-09-28 | **A published figure is not mechanically tied to a recorded result** — Filed 2026-09-28 by VM1.3. `result.validate` and `core.eval.resultsink` now refuse a single run of any quantity that varies between runs, but a figure reaches `docs/metrics-baseline.md` by hand. Nothing checks that each figure there cites a row in a results file (committed or attached as a CI artefact, VM1.5) that passed those checks, so a single-run number typed into the baseline would be caught only in review. A figure cites its row next to the number, `1.80x <sub>[ev:<digest> n=<N>]</sub>`, where the digest is the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the row's canonical JSON, so a cited row cannot be edited; `/ci` cites an interval, `/saving` a ratio printed as a percentage saved. **The check.** `scripts/check_figure_evidence.py`, in the quality gate's checks step: every section of `docs/metrics-baseline.md` that prints a figure opens with a printed marker, `**Evidence: verified.**`, `legacy, unverified`, `withdrawn` or `not a measurement` with its reason. Mutants of the checker, each killed: value comparison disabled (3 failures), missing-citation rule disabled (3), `/ci` rule disabled (1), legacy date rule disabled (1); restored and checked with `cmp`. **Not done:** (1) 146 figures in seven sections remain legacy, unverified until re-measured through the sink with BCa; the throughput and AD1.3 blocks need a model or the measuring host. (2) Append-only is checked against HEAD only; an amended or rewritten commit is caught in review, not by the check. ## Epic CB1: Correctness Benchmark — Three Arms

*Prove that a no-custody architecture can do the work, or find out that it cannot. Depends on VM1 and research spike RS3.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| CB1.1 | M | **Done** | **Define the three arms, and the honest framing** — (A) data in the prompt; (B) schema only, model answers directly; (C) schema only, model returns an artifact, loke executes locally. State which model does what in each arm: arm C does not use a *local* model for generation at all, only for custody, which answers the "handicapped by weak local models" objection. **Framing constraint:** the arm-C data flow is not novel — it is how every text-to-SQL benchmark already works and it ships in several commercial products (`docs/research/disclosure-measurement-findings.md` §10). This epic measures the **cost** of strict no-custody, candidly, and should be expected to lose ground on some question classes; it does not claim the architecture as an invention. |
| CB1.2 | L |  | **Execution-based scoring harness** — Primary benchmark: **InfiAgent-DABench** (257 closed-form questions over 52 CSV files, Apache-2.0, Python sandbox), because it is the only candidate where paste-the-data is the honest status-quo baseline; on the text-to-SQL suites schema-only is already the norm, so measuring there proves nothing. Score by executing the result with a gold-executability invariant asserted first. **257 items gives roughly ±6 pp binomial confidence, so comparisons must be paired on identical items and tested with McNemar, not as two independent proportions.** Secondary: BIRD Mini-Dev (500 items), noting its efficiency metric is computed only over queries that pass execution accuracy and is therefore not comparable across systems with different accuracy. **Avoid Spider 2.0-Snow** — audited annotation-error rate 62.8–66.1%. |
| CB1.2a | M |  | **Freeze the output-contract reformat step — largest validity threat** — DABench post-processes model output into its answer template with a separate reformat model, and that step is worth **up to 32 accuracy points** (Mistral-7B 6.23 → 38.67; GPT-4 72.76 → 78.99). That is larger than any plausible effect of the disclosure regime under test. If arm C returns a structured spec (naturally parseable) and arm A returns prose with an embedded answer, the experiment measures format compliance and calls it privacy-preserving correctness. The reformat step must be **identical, frozen and applied symmetrically to every arm**, and both reformat-on and reformat-off numbers reported. |
| CB1.3 | M | **Done** | **Output-contract control** — Adherence to the required output format materially changes scores on published analysis benchmarks, so the contract must be treated as a controlled variable and reported, not left implicit. |
| CB1.4 | M |  | **Pre-empt the corrected-benchmark critique** — Published benchmarks carry large annotation-error rates (BIRD Mini-Dev 52.8%; Spider 2.0-Snow 62.8–66.1%), moving scores by −7% to 31% and rankings by up to nine positions across 16 re-evaluated agents. Cite the journal version (arXiv:2601.08778 = PVLDB 19(5)), not only the workshop precursor. **loke's cheaper and stronger pre-emption:** because the comparison is within-benchmark and paired — same question, same data, two disclosure regimes — annotation errors are a *shared* confound that largely cancels in the difference. Say so, then report paired deltas rather than leaderboard absolutes, hand-audit a stratified sample of ~100 items, publish the audit, and report raw and audited subsets separately. |
| CB1.5 | M |  | **Cost and token accounting per arm** — Tokens per completed task against arm A as the named baseline. This is what makes "minimising token spend" falsifiable; today no baseline workload is defined anywhere. |
| CB1.6 | M |  | **Position against the closest prior art on its own datasets** — The nearest work formalises minimisation as an ordinal lattice over per-entity actions (retain, abstract, redact) and searches it under a utility floor, but **every point in that lattice still sends data to the model**. loke's no-custody path sits outside it, made feasible by moving the computation rather than the data (`docs/research/disclosure-measurement-findings.md` §5). That is a real contribution **only if** loke demonstrates comparable utility at a comparable operating point **on the same datasets** that work uses; anything less reads as redacting everything and losing the task. Also reuse its two black-box recovery audits verbatim so loke's numbers are directly comparable to a published baseline. Schema-only prompting is already standard in text-to-SQL — cite it as support, do not deny it. Depends on RS4. |

## Epic GA5: Assurance Evidence

*Make the audit trail something an assessor could actually rely on, and be precise about what it does and does not evidence.*

| Story | Size | Status | Summary |
|-------|------|--------|---------|
| GA5.1 | S | **Done** | **Fix audit timestamps** — `packages/core/src/storage/audit.tk:47` writes the **string literal** `'now()'` into `created_at`, so every row carries the same seven characters instead of a time. `ORDER BY created_at` is therefore undefined and the period filters in `packages/core/src/governance/dashboard.tk:63,75,86,97` cannot work. Without a time basis there is no period, and without a period there is no evidence of a control operating *over* one.<br><br>**Status detail:** **Done** — `created_at` is a real epoch-ms from `db.nowms`, and the chain-tail query orders `created_at DESC, rowid DESC` so same-millisecond rows still order deterministically |
| GA5.2 | M | **Done** | **Real hash chain** — `audit.tk:38` computes `hash = str.concat(correlationid, eventtype)`. That is not a hash, it covers none of the payload, and `prev_hash` is stored but is **not an input**, so nothing chains. Compute a cryptographic digest over a canonical serialisation of every persisted field **including the previous row's hash**, using an unambiguous field separator and a defined genesis value. toke provides `crypto.sha256`, `crypto.tohex` and `crypto.constanteq`.<br><br>**Status detail:** **Done** — `eventdigest(prevhash;id;event;created)` sha256s the previous hash plus all fourteen fields. Tamper and gap detection are still unasserted: that is GA5.3 |

Mutants: JSON escaping removed (`jx.escape` replaced by bare quoting): `smoke_report.sh` "JSON with a quote, comma, newline and backslash in its fields parses, and each comes back exact" and the unit "JSON carries the rows, with every string escaped" failed; CSV quoting removed (`csvfield` never quotes): `smoke_report.sh` "CSV with the same row parses as RFC 4180: one record of five fields, each exact" and the unit "CSV quotes a field holding a comma, quote or newline, and doubles the quote inside it" failed; each restored, `cmp` identical. (2) `kill_switch_agent_refused` is in no template: agents send nothing to a model yet (executor, LLM stubbed); when they do, a template should say how agent runs are counted. (3) the CSV records end in LF, not RFC 4180's CRLF; Python's reader and spreadsheets accept both, and the CLI adds a final newline of its own. |

(6) `score_patterns.py` does not read the new patterns.<br><br>**Update 2026-10-01: the UK and Singapore identifiers (Not done item 3).** Five regex detectors, each RESTRICTED in the layer and in `core.privacy.pipeline`'s `maxsensitivity`/`countrestricted`, each validated only as far as a published specification allows (cited in `patterns.tkc.md`): `uk_nhs_number` (ten digits, NHS Data Dictionary modulus 11 with 11 -> 0 and 10 never issued, `regex.nhschecksumvalid`; ALSO gated on the word NHS, because about one in eleven bare ten-digit runs, Australian mobiles and US 3-3-4 numbers, would pass the check and raise the prompt to RESTRICTED); `uk_nino` (two letters, six digits, A-D, optionally spaced in pairs; HMRC NIM39110's letter and prefix rules in `regex.ninovalid`; no check digit exists; unlabelled, with a letter or digit on either side rejecting it); `uk_sort_code` (nn-nn-nn after `sort code`; no check digit, so gated on its words as BSB is, rejecting only 00-00-00); `uk_driving_licence` (DVLA leaflet INS57P's sixteen characters: surname padded with 9, decade, month or month+50, day, year, initials; `regex.ukdrivinglicencevalid`; the three check characters are randomly generated per the leaflet and not judged); `sg_nric` (S/T/F/G/M, seven digits and a letter, after NRIC, FIN or NRIC/FIN). **The NRIC check letter is NOT validated:** the ICA does not publish the algorithm; the one in circulation is reverse engineered (Ngiam 2003, which records it is released only to Singapore organisations on application) and accounts of the 2022 M series disagree, so it is gated on its words as CRN is. `core.privacy.entityvocab` maps them to `nhs_number`, `nino` and `national_id`, `sort_code` and `financial`, `uk_driving_licence` and `drivers_licence`, `nric` and `national_id`; all five left `undetected`. NHS, NINO, driver number and NRIC are scored as direct identifiers (`evaluation.isdirectidentifier`). Harness CASES carry one value each. **Found by the gate's privacy harness and fixed:** an NHS number printed 3-3-4 is also a `phone_us` match with the same value, and `pipeline.dedupentities` keeps the first of two equal values, so the pipeline kept the phone number and rated the prompt CONFIDENTIAL; `uk_nhs_number` now comes before the phone patterns in `getpatterns` (asserted: deduplicated, the NHS number survives and the prompt is RESTRICTED). The dedup rule itself (first equal value wins, regardless of sensitivity) is unchanged and is filed as RG1.7c. **Corpus:** 24 cases appended to `generate.py` (the first 122 byte-identical, checked with `cmp`): 3 NHS, 3 NINO, 2 sort code, 3 driver number and 3 NRIC/FIN positives, and 10 near misses (a checksum-valid ten digits without NHS, a wrong check digit, a check of 10, HMRC's own specimen QQ123456C, prefix GB, a NINO inside a longer token, a date nn-nn-nn, sort code 00-00-00, a driver-number shape with month 42, an NRIC shape without its words). **Measured** (regex layer, `test_detection_recall.tk`, 146-case corpus, not published to metrics-baseline): before, recall 91.72% (133/145; two NHS numbers were caught only by `phone_us`), direct 100.00% (81/81, the new types not yet direct), 144 regions, 11 false positives (92.36%), exact-span 86.21%; after, recall 100.00% (145/145), direct 100.00% (93/93), 155 regions, 10 false positives (93.55%), exact-span 94.48%. No near miss is reported. Floors unchanged at 99.00% (93 of 93: losing one fails). **Evidence:** `tests/unit/privacy/test_uk_sg_identifiers.tk` (new: per detector the forms, value, span, sensitivity, one rejection per validation rule, the context guard, fragments, and the pipeline's rating); `test_entity_vocab.tk` (the five leave `undetected` and hit uk-gdpr's and sg-pdpa's blocks); `test_regex_detector.tk` (22 patterns); `test_preset_detection.tk` now also covers uk-gdpr and sg-pdpa, and names the five in `required`. **Mutants** (one build, distinct assertions; restored, `cmp` identical): NHS check removed (3 assertions: wrong check digit, check of 10, predicate); NINO unused-prefix and suffix rules removed (2: prefix GB, predicate; the first/second-letter rule was not mutated); sort code all-zero rejection removed (1); driver-number structure removed (5: month 13, month 63, day 00, letter after a 9, predicate); NRIC words removed (1: the context guard). Corpus precision under the mutant fell to 89.51% (17 false positives). **Still not done:** the special categories and biometric (item 1), password and health (2), the four AU detectors' unlabelled forms (4), unenforced presets (5), `score_patterns.py` (6); also an NHS number, sort code or NRIC without its words, Scottish CHI and Northern Irish H&C numbers, and the NRIC check letter. |

Build it so it respects sensitivity (a request may only fall back to a model allowed its level), surface the degraded mode to the user, and record entry and exit so a disruption can be measured against tolerance. Acceptance: a test with a provider that fails, asserting a local answer, a visible degraded marker and a recorded event. What was missing: no chain the router BUILT ever held a local hop after a cloud first choice. With `prefer_local` on, a cloud first choice means no local model met the first choice's latency tier, so every later hop was cloud too; nothing marked a degraded answer; nothing recorded a disruption. **Built.** *The hop:* `core.router.router.routechain` ends a cloud-first chain that holds no local hop with `degradehop`: a local model chosen by `routedecided` (the same selector and the same RESTRICTED check as every hop) from the catalogue without the models already seen, with `prefer_local` on and the background tier, so a local model too slow for the first choice's tier still qualifies. It is tried only after every cloud hop has failed or been refused, and may make the chain one hop longer than `maxhops`. A local model is permitted at every sensitivity, so the hop never widens where the prompt may go. `routechainpreferinstalled` keeps the installed-only chain when both it and the full-catalogue chain choose a cloud model first (their cloud hops are the same), so the degrade hop is a model Ollama has. *Marker:* `core.router.degraded` (new). A browser reply answered this way carries `"degraded":true` and `"degraded_from":"<provider:model>"` beside `answered_by`, and the chat page shows a note under the answer; `loke ask` prints `degraded: <provider:model> did not answer, so a local model (...) did`. *Record:* the first degraded answer for a provider writes an `audit_log` row `degraded_mode_entered` (provider, the local model, the request's correlation id) and keeps the start in settings (`routing.degraded.<provider>.since`, ms); further degraded answers add nothing; the next answer from that provider writes `degraded_mode_exited` whose `duration_ms` is the disruption's length, and clears the start. A local first choice is never degraded and never ends a disruption. **Approval (GA5.26, F5.3a), measured, rule unchanged:** `approval_destination` refuses a cloud-to-local hop for a request held for approval. It never meets a degrade hop in production: `core.governance.policy` asks for approval only for HIGH risk over RESTRICTED data, and RESTRICTED data is never routed to a cloud model first, so an approved request has no cloud first choice to degrade from. A request that can go to the cloud first is not held, so the approval check passes its degrade hop. Asserted against the production `decide` and router. **Evidence:** `tests/integration/test_degrade_local.tk` (new, 29 assertions), against `scripts/lib/http_recorder.py` stand-ins (an Ollama with qwen2.5:72b installed, an answering and a silent Anthropic; OpenAI has no client on this path, so its hop is refused in-process). The chain is the production one, `routechainpreferinstalled` with the browser path's own configuration: a code review at instant tolerance goes to `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5` first and ends with `ollama:qwen2.5:72b` (control: with no installed local code reviewer there is no degrade hop; a local first choice gets none). Walked by `walkchainat`: the silent provider receives the request, the local model answers, the reply is 200 with `answered_by` the local model, `degraded` and `degraded_from`, and one entry row is written; a second degraded answer writes no second row; the provider answering again gives an unmarked reply and one exit row with its duration. The same through `dispatchchain` for `loke ask`. **Mutant** (file kept outside the tree, restored, verified with `cmp`): with `routechain`'s degrade branch disabled (`if(firstlocal \|\| anylocal(hops))` made `if(true)`), 11 assertions of `test_degrade_local.tk` failed, first "A CLOUD-FIRST CHAIN ENDS WITH THE LOCAL MODEL IT DEGRADES TO" (`openai:gpt-4o` != `ollama:qwen2.5:72b`), then the full-catalogue chain, the local hop never sent, "WHEN THE CLOUD PROVIDER FAILS, THE LOCAL MODEL ANSWERS (got 502)", "THE REPLY IS MARKED DEGRADED", and the entry and exit rows. The unmutated control passed. **Not done:** (1) No tolerance is configured or checked: the rows make a disruption measurable, nothing compares it with a CPS 230 tolerance (RG1.2 Not done 3). (2) Local inference has not run on target hardware (LC1). (3) No HTTP smoke of a degraded reply over the built binary: the Anthropic endpoint cannot be stood in for in the binary (F5.3a), so the cloud hop is covered by the integration test only. (4) The CPS 230 preset's `cps230-degrade-to-local` rule stays `UNIMPLEMENTED`: its text and the preset's local-provider note no longer say nothing retries a failed call locally, but no field of the preset governs the path and no tolerance is checked, so it was not reclassified (RG1.2's call). |
